# A Philosophical and Chemical
## Treatise: titled

# The Little Peasant:

## Hitherto long hidden, and also
### withheld and falsified by some
### out of spite:

->Now, however<-

Brought forth in its entirety from the Arnsburg Library of the Most Reverend Lord Ernest, Elector and Bishop of Cologne <note>Ernest of Bavaria (1554–1612), who was a notable patron of alchemy</note>.

## Concerning the <term>Matter</term> and Knowledge of the
## single and true <term>Great Universal Subject</term>, and
## its preparation: Which precedes all Tinctures of the
### whole of Chemistry: and from whose Spirit all things of the world
->Universally originate and<-
->flow forth.<-

## Together with the added Commentaries of JOHANN
->W A L C H of Schondorf.<-

Wherein the actual and steadfast opinions of all true <term>philosophers</term> <note>In this context, "philosophers" refers specifically to alchemists or "philosophers of nature"</note> are demonstrated in a <term>compendium</term> and brief summary, with true natural foundations and entirely intelligible reasons, and set before the eyes of all <term>Sons of Doctrine</term> <note>original Latin: "Doctrinæ filijs"; a traditional alchemical term for dedicated students of the art</note>.

Also attached is an Epistle to all the Philosophers of Germany:
*Cleansed and fixed spirits are the most ready*

## Treatise: titled

# The Little Peasant:

## Hitherto long hidden, and also
### withheld and falsified by some
### out of spite:

->Now, however<-

Brought forth in its entirety from the Arnsburg Library of the Most Reverend Lord Ernest, Elector and Bishop of Cologne <note>Ernest of Bavaria (1554–1612), an influential prince-bishop and a significant patron of alchemical research</note>.

->W A L C H of Schondorf.<-

# The Little Peasant.

It is an old saying or common proverb <note>original: *Proverbium*</note> among us Germans: After great suffering commonly comes great joy / and so also the reverse: <note>original Latin: *Sic & è contra*</note> So it went for me as well, unfortunately, a few years ago / (it has likely happened to others too / who began without a true ground or foundation / almost the same way) as I will recount at length. For when I believed I held the entire world in my hand / I received less than nothing. Because my glass <note>the alchemical vessel or flask</note> / in which I had now placed my entire well-being / shattered with a loud crack; the materials splattered my "silent philosophers" <note>original Latin: *Mutos philosophos*—this likely refers to his alchemical books or symbolic illustrations that "speak" through images rather than words</note> and books here and there with great damage and loss / of which I must now forbear to mention further. Only that I was so frozen / silenced / and terrified by this unexpected misfortune / to such an extent / that out of grief and distress I knew not where I was / what I intended to do / and how I should proceed further. Accordingly, my joy / delight / and bliss had transmuted <note>original: *transmutiert*</note> and changed into nothing but poison and bitter sauces / and not into gold and silver (as I had hoped).

<page-num>11</page-num>
# The Peasant

Take therefore these two lilies, completely and purely polished, and enclose them in a crystal [vessel], sealed tight against the fire; <note>The text suggests a hermetic seal—sealing a glass vessel with a torch so that no "spirits" or vapors can escape during heating.</note> place them in a gentle **sweat-bath** <term>sweat-bath: also known as a *balneum Mariae*, this is a water bath used to provide steady, indirect, and gentle heat.</term>, so that the **white lily** will spread out wide and take the **red one** into itself and enclose it. Because the Red is of a fiery nature and finds help from the external warmth, let it also release its hot balsamic scent out into the cold of the White. Through this, they become at odds, for neither will yield or give way to the other; this is caused by their **opposing qualities** <note>original Latin: *Contrariæ qualitates*</note>, as you well know. Both grow toward the heavens but are driven down again by the wind—and this happens several times until they are weary, tired, and exhausted from the labor of rising and falling, and must rest upon the earth. <note>This "rising and falling" describes the process of circulation or distillation within a closed vessel, where vapors rise, condense, and drip back down.</note>

And know that if the bath is not governed in such a way that both natures rise together, but only one alone, you will never enjoy their scent nor partake of it; therefore, pay close attention to this remarkable **operation**.

But because these two enemies now perceive and notice that one can do nothing against the other, they unite again with such love and friendship that they henceforth desire to remain together eternally.

In this union, the entire **firmament** <note>In alchemy, the "firmament" often refers to the upper part of the glass vessel, which acts as a miniature sky where vapors (the "stars") gather.</note> is moved, likewise the **Sun and Moon**, to such an extent that they are both eclipsed for as long as it pleases the Most High. <note>The "eclipse" of the Sun and Moon represents the *nigredo* or "blackness" stage, where the matter decays and turns dark before it can be purified.</note> After this, God the Almighty, out of love, creates His **bow** <note>This refers to the "Peacock’s Tail" (*cauda pavonis*), a stage where the matter in the vessel displays a shimmering array of colors like a rainbow.</note> in the air, and
all kinds...

This Moon becomes violently vexed because of the union of the other planets—to such an extent that it turns yellowish out of its anger and finally becomes **blood-red**. But because she <note>The Moon is personified as female here.</note> humbles herself before him <note>The Sun is personified as male.</note> as her Lord (for God has so ordained it), he receives her back into grace and makes her equal to him, so that she may remain and rule with him forever in his kingdom. For this, they may all rightly rejoice, giving thanks and praise—after him—to God the Most High, by whose permission they are so heartily adorned and gifted. They also hope to daily merit and employ such adornment for the praise of His Divine Name.

Regarding my wisdom, I have it from Him alone, through whose Word and Command heaven and earth must tremble and shake. As a result, I have already told you that I am inwardly adorned with gold, diamonds, emeralds, and rubies, and have only belted this gray smock around me to hide myself from the powerful (for they intend to capture and compel me).

I spoke further: Why do the great lords and potentates not seek this <term>Philosophy: In this context, "Philosophy" refers to Alchemy or the "Great Work"—the secret knowledge of nature's inner workings and the transformation of matter.</term> from their philosophers, whom they must maintain annually at the universities with great salaries? He answered: I could discourse on this question <note>original Latin: *quæstion*</note> for a long time. After I had now thanked, lauded, and praised from my heart the Eternal, alone-powerful God and Creator of all things for His gracious revelation: Then I took my **Second Matter** <term>Materia secunda: In alchemical theory, this is the substance after it has undergone its first stage of preparation or "awakening," moving it closer to becoming the Philosopher's Stone.</term> to myself (**First Matter** <term>Prima materia: The "First Matter" or raw, chaotic substance found in nature that serves as the starting point for the alchemical Great Work.</term> will follow later), and kissed it for joy, as that for which I had such a heartfelt yearning and desire, and for whose sake I had stood for so many years in doubt, tribulation, sadness, and distress. Then it occurred to me that the Peasant <note>The "Bawr" or Peasant is a recurring symbolic figure in this text who provides spiritual and alchemical secrets.</note> had said that God did this for very important reasons, and also so that the poor as well as the rich might have it, and would have no cause to complain or lament against God as if He had given the rich a preference in this matter. No, truly, the rich do not respect it, and believe much less that such a thing resides within it, as is to be read in the **Great Rosary** <note>original: *Rosario Magno*. This refers to the *Rosarium philosophorum*, one of the most famous illustrated alchemical manuscripts of the 16th century.</note> on page 248:

> If we called our Matter by its own name, the foolish and the rich would not believe it to be so. <note>original Latin: *Si Materia nostram nomine nuncuparemus suo, Insipientes & Divites eam esse non crederent*.</note>

Also, the poor obtain it sooner than the rich.

Once I had well wrapped and secured my **Matter** <term>Materia: The physical substance used as the starting point for the alchemical work.</term>, I went back home with joy and sang the following little song on the way.

I had not been home long when I resolved first to prepare a reasonable supply of funds from the **Particular** <term>The Particular: In alchemy, a "particular" refers to a lesser process that transmutes specific metals into gold or silver, used here by the author to fund the long and expensive "Universal" work.</term>, as the kind Peasant had taught me, so that I could attend to the preparation of the **Universal** <term>The Universal: The "Great Work" or the creation of the Philosopher's Stone, which was intended to have a universal effect on all health and metals.</term> with better peace and stability. Therefore, I began in God’s name, bought a considerable supply of coal (for it takes much coal), built serviceable furnaces and ovens for this purpose, and in a short time produced a considerable supply.

The Enemy of Christians could not suffer such a thing and incited one disturbance after another. The neighbors complained against me, fearing I would set their houses on fire. My friends and other acquaintances reproached me, saying there were counterfeiters <note>original: *Müntzer*. Because alchemists worked with furnaces and metals, they were frequently suspected of illegal coining.</note> about. They told me I should desist from such vain undertakings so that I would not fall under suspicion, and should instead more earnestly pursue my **legal profession** <note>original: *facultatem juridicam*.</note>, since I was a **Doctor of Law** <note>original: *Doctor Juris*.</note>, and attend to its duties; I would surely be able to have my ample sustenance from this. But whether I could thereby earn my bread with a good conscience, I—alas—very much doubted. The worst was that the common blacksmiths and goldsmiths complained about me before the Council, saying that I made the coal expensive for them, so that they could not carry on their craft and civic livelihood, and **consequently** <note>original: *per consequentiam*.</note> were unable to pay the Council and the common City—

I paid neither interest nor tax, yet I paid dearly for the coal just to ensure I could have it before they did. They kept this up for so long that even the City Council sent word to forbid me from such things, indicating that I should **cease the handling of coal** <note>original: *à tractatione carbonum*</note> and instead conduct myself according to my professional calling. In short, there was so much commotion that I was forced to tear down my furnaces, move away from that place, and seek out a good friend who would provide me with enough funds so that I might await the **Universal** <term>Universal: The "Great Work," the ultimate alchemical goal of creating the Philosopher's Stone which could transform any metal.</term> more peacefully; yet I told no one what I had in mind. Those same **tribulations** <note>original: *tribulationes*</note>, involving travels and other inconveniences, lasted nearly three years. God knows how it grieved my heart that, though I knew and was capable of everything, I still could not set my hand to the work. # Commentaries #
<note>original: "Commentaria"</note>

...which makes other **vegetation** <note>original: "Vegetabilia"</note> grow. Regarding the gnats that, at the beginning of winter, shut themselves away between the walls, in the cracks and stains of the masonry, in churches and other buildings—I believe that they eventually die, and the living spirit within them is extinguished, so that they lie there dead. But when the warmth returns in the spring, a little spark from the life-giving universal **spirit of nature** <note>original: "allgemeinen Geist der Natur"</note> comes into them again from the outside, so that their tinder receives something from this; and, because they were previously disposed toward this, the spirit seeks out its old **dwelling** <note>original: "domicilium"</note> again, and they are brought back and awakened from death to their former life. # On the Little Creature <note>original: "öber den kleinen Bawren." While "Bauer" usually means "peasant" or "farmer," in this period it could also refer to a "builder" or an "inhabitant" of a physical frame or structure.</note>

... we desire to instill a soul and a life into the **prepared body** <note>original: *disponierten Corpori*; referring to the cast metal form of the insect</note>; that, however, is God’s work alone. We now discuss among ourselves the question: from where does the life of such little creatures—the **insects** <note>original: *Infectis*</note>—come, and how is it poured into them? Namely, it comes from the **life-giving spirit**, which is indeed scattered everywhere in the air and slips into the nearest **prepared body** <note>original: *disponierte Corpus*</note>, but in our chest <note>the internal cavity of a being</note> it is condensed. The entire world, however, is full of this **vital spirit** <note>original: *Spiritus vitalis*; the breath of life believed to animate all matter</note>.

A **philosopher** <note>original: *Philosophus*</note> said in times past—just as the **Brahmins** <note>original: *Brachmanni*</note>, the Indian philosophers, also expressed it: "The world is an animal." He did not speak this out of ignorance. You see how this animal breathes, what a strong breath it lets out and in everywhere, how all the limbs of this animal move; there is nothing but spirit and life within it. Consider also what **reason** <note>original: *ration*</note>, craftsmanship, order, and wonderful, inscrutable nature and property it has in all its works and deeds.

# About the Small Peasant <note>The "Small Peasant" (*Der kleine Bauer*) refers to a famous alchemical treatise, often attributed to Johann Grasshoff, which used agricultural metaphors to describe chemical processes.</note>

Nevertheless, here in our **Work of Nature** <term>Work of Nature: the alchemical process viewed as a natural growth rather than a forced chemical reaction</term>, a preparation must take place, and the field must be made ready for the future fruit and planting.

Indeed, just as it is accustomed to happen with other plants: that one must help them at the beginning and set them in motion; which, once they are planted and placed in the refined, cultivated, or tilled ground, subsequently arrange themselves quite finely on their own, without the aid of a human hand or any applied medicine <note>In this context, "medicine" refers to external chemical additives or unnecessary interventions</note>, if one only grants them air and removes every hindrance from their path. When they have good weather, proper moisture, and pleasant warmth for the **decoction** <term>Decoction: translated from "Außkochung," referring to the internal ripening or "cooking" of the plant's juices through steady heat</term>, they proceed in growth and increase, moving from color to color, stretching themselves daily with power toward **maturation** <term>Maturation: the process of ripening or reaching chemical perfection</term>, until they become ripe, taking on the colors almost in the aforementioned order; for that is the true natural transformation of the same. Finally, out of a thing that was initially raw, harsh, unrefined, sour, and tasteless—a mixed **Chaos** <term>Chaos: the confused, undifferentiated initial state of primordial matter</term>—a timely, beautiful, flavorful, well-colored, and healthy fruit reveals itself to the laboring man, liberated and separated from its husk, and falls off or away by itself quite cleanly, provided one only holds the hat <note>A metaphorical reference to the collecting vessel or the "helm" of a still used to catch the final product</note> underneath so that it does not perish.

<summary>This page uses a botanical metaphor to explain that alchemy is a natural process; once the "field" is prepared, the matter matures through various colors like a ripening fruit. The alchemist's role is compared to a gardener who provides the right conditions—warmth and air—while Nature performs the actual transformation.</summary>

# Commentaries

If any natural thing exists in the world, then the completion <note>original: "Außfertigung"</note> and the mastery <term>Mastery: translated from "Magisterium," a term for the completed alchemical process or the "Great Work" itself</term> of our Philosophers' Stone is natural, and not the work of a man, but entirely the work of Nature. The Artist <term>Artist: a common term for the alchemist, implying one who practices the "Art" of transformation</term> adds nothing to it, except solely that he directs Nature toward growth (just as any farmer or vinedresser <note>original: "Rebmann"</note> does with his fruits and plantings), clears all hindrances—as mentioned—out of the way, and is so keen in understanding, and possesses such great grace from God, that he governs its course and, when necessary, applies a bit <note>original: "Gebiß"; a bridle or bit used to control a horse, used here metaphorically for restraining or moderating the chemical process</note>.

For God implanted such power into this creature <note>here referring to the "prime matter" or the substance of the Stone</note> above all other creatures at the very beginning of Creation, and still endows it daily; were that not so, it would be impossible for any human on earth to bring such a work to its desired end, or to create any benefit here. Also, since He endowed man with reason <note>original: "Vernunfft"</note> above all other animals, so that he might recognize His works and not leave them uninvestigated: it is right for this man, and those whom He awakens for it, to take up this high and deeply hidden work and great secret, to seek this treasure <note>original: "Schatz"</note>, to open the chest, and to the glory and honor of his Creator, to bring forth the most precious pearl <note>original: "Berlen"</note> and noblest essence that Nature has ever kept hidden within her as long as the world has stood—to enjoy it, to apply it to the welfare <note>original: "Wolfahrt"</note> of the needy, and to offer Him eternal praise and thanks.

-ents: For no thing can bring itself forth / *for like does not act upon like* <note>original Latin: *simile namque non agit in sibi simile*</note>. Now when an active principle <note>German: *Wirckents*</note> finds itself in the *object* or the passive principle <note>German: *Leidenden*</note> / and follows its orderly course / it gives birth at the end of the work to a third thing / and brings a new form and *essence* <note>original Latin/German: *Essents*</note> / and then the active is entirely separated from the passive / or from the new form that has been introduced / and then a completed work stands upon the place.

That is the *sublimation of the philosophers* <note>original Latin: *philosophorum sublimation*. In alchemy, this refers to the purification and elevation of a substance to a higher state.</note>.

...[sti]ck as well in this root, as **Sol [Gold]** and **Luna [Silver]**: they are also born out of this root. The only difference is that the lesser and imperfect planets <note>In alchemy, "planets" refers to the base metals: Lead (Saturn), Tin (Jupiter), Iron (Mars), and Copper (Venus).</note> do not achieve maturity and full cooking, but instead stall along the way and mix and unite with the outer **Sulfur**, in whose womb they lie; and this happens in various ways, according to what companion the **Mercury** finds.

For as soon as the active principle mixes with the passive <note>German: *Leydenden*, literally "the suffering" or "the patient" principle that receives action</note>—which usually happens before the full cooking is complete and the goal cannot be reached—it results in an imperfect birth and does not reach the goal for which it originally aimed. For the *end* <term>finis</term> of every *digestion* <term>digestion: the alchemical process of breaking down and maturing a substance through gentle, continuous heat</term> is the introduction and birth of a new essence within that same matter.

...give off a lovely scent to the one who breaks them off with washed hands.

**Folio 5.** This little peasant makes a fine distinction between the **First Matter** <term>First Matter: also called "Materia Prima," the primordial, undifferentiated substance from which all things are created</term> and the **Second Matter** <term>Second Matter: matter that has already begun to take on specific characteristics or has undergone its first stage of processing</term>, and gives his student good instruction regarding this.

Not everyone who takes up **Alchemy** <note>original: "Chemiæ"</note> and the philosophical work understands immediately what the **Philosophers** <note>In alchemical texts, "Philosophers" refers to the sages and masters of the alchemical art</note> call their **First Matter** <note>original: "primam materiam"</note>. This task requires a sharp mind and a keen, even complete understanding of the entire work; it requires a man who is experienced in the **Universal** <term>Universal: the "Great Work" or the overarching process that governs all of nature from beginning to end</term> from the beginning to the end.

When one speaks of the **First Matter of the Philosophers** <note>original: "Materia prima philosophorum"</note>, the common laboratory worker or **student** <note>original: "Studiosus"</note> immediately understands it to be the first **subject** <note>original: "Subjectum," meaning the physical raw material</note> that the **Craftsman** <note>original: "Artifex"</note> takes in hand—the **primary matter** <note>original: "primum hyle"</note> or the "mountain" which is said to contain the aforementioned **Vital Spirit** <note>original: "Spiritum vitalem," the life force or animating essence within matter</note>. All creatures **participate** in this spirit, and it is from this very substance that the **Stone** <term>The Stone: the Philosopher's Stone, the goal of the alchemical quest</term> itself must be made.

And in this matter, everyone has their own narrow **Subject** and fantasy that they imagine for themselves to be the **First Matter**. However, these are commonly useless, clumsy things for such a trade, in which no possibility of success is found.

When it thunders, lightens, strikes, and rumbles, it happens because the work has been overdriven, the **place** <note>original: *locus*</note> is too narrow, and too much heat is applied; strong trapped heat and surrounding cold fight with one another, and the process proceeds with violence and is pushed too far. For there, **contrary qualities** <note>original: *contrariæ qualitates*</note> are found which cannot tolerate each other; therefore, it must either have air, or the glass will swell and burst, or develop cracks.

### Commentaries

...but rather the materials <note>original: *Materialia*</note> from which one wishes to make and compose the Stone [the Philosopher's Stone] must enter the helm <note>original: *Helm*; the cap or upper part of a still or alembic</note> at the same time, and likewise and all at once run out together through the beak <note>the spout of the alembic</note> of the helm at the front. We shall leave it at that.

The second [point], he says, is the Resolution <term>Resolution|The process of breaking down a solid substance into its constituent parts, typically by dissolving it into a liquid</term>, which he also values greatly, though the Philosophers <note>referring to the traditional alchemical authorities</note> do not say many words about it.

In the Work, there is not just one kind of Resolution. First, it is that one brings a body <note>original: *Corpus*; the solid physical matter</note> into a liquid substance. Secondly, it is that one leads the water back again onto its earth <note>original: *Terrá*</note>, whereby one then makes it soft and approaches the spirit <note>original: *spiritui*</note> ever more closely; and that is properly the solution of the earth <note>original: *solutio terræ*</note>. Finally, there is also a Solution where the subject <note>the primary material of the work</note> reveals itself, Sun and Moon <note>symbolizing Gold and Silver, or the masculine and feminine principles</note> become one body, and the snake sheds its old skin in which it was stuck this past year, and is divested of all earthly and coarse nature, and rejuvenates itself; of this, Rhazes <note>original: *Rasis*; a celebrated 9th-century Persian physician and alchemist</note> says:

> *If you are ignorant of the true dissolution of our body, there is no reason for you to work; for if that is unknown, the rest will be useless.* <note>original Latin: "Si veram nostri corporis dissolutionem ignoraveris, non est quòd opereris, illa siquidem ignota, reliquum inutile fuerit."</note>

These can all be called solutions <note>original: *solutiones*</note>. Finally, there is yet another Solution, which we do not treat in this book: where one dissolves the cooked in the raw <note>original: *coctum in crudo*; a reference to a specific advanced stage of the process</note>. However, we wish to understand it here simply and plainly as the first dissolution and preparation <note>original: *Præparation*</note> of the subject, for first of all, everything must become water and a liquor, so that the four elements may, in such a way,

And it does this of its own accord; thus, a redness must surely have been hidden behind or beneath it from the beginning. For the yellow has helped to ripen the **Mercury** <note>original: *Mercurium*</note> up to this point, and has [helped] it onto its feet...

### Commentaries

...rising up, and how should one behave there? Of this a philosopher speaks: *Make the woman ascend over the male, and the male shall ascend over the woman.* <note>original Latin: *Fac ascendere fœminam super masculum : & ascendet masculus super fœminam.* This describes the interaction of volatile and fixed substances.</note> 

Contrive so that the woman (who is **Mercury** <term>Mercurius|The alchemical principle of fluidity, volatility, and the feminine spirit</term>) lies on top and climbs upon the man (who is the red **Sulfur** <term>Sulphur|The alchemical principle of combustibility, structure, and the masculine soul</term>, which one finds in the Swiss mountains, in the **Alps** <note>original: *Alpibus*</note>, up toward the heights of **Graubünden** <note>A mountainous region in eastern Switzerland, historically known for its mineral deposits.</note>). Then, in turn, the man will climb upon the woman. Yes, this occurs if it happens by the counsel of the **Artist** <term>Artist|A common term for the alchemist or practitioner of the 'Hermetic Art'</term>, who must hold the stirrup for him.

For there are two distinct works: first, bringing the woman upon the man happens with long and cautious labor. But then, in turn, leaving space for the man and "arming" him so that he masters the woman requires a different manual skill. It is no minor task, but a mightily difficult thing and a weighty work; in this labor, many have gone astray, and it proceeds by **coagulating** <term>Coagulation|The process of thickening or solidifying a liquid into a mass</term> and **calcining** <term>Calcination|The reduction of a substance to powder or ash through intense heat</term>.

Then, what you have done until now, do now quickly in reverse. That is: if you have **dissolved** <note>original: *solviert*</note> until now, then coagulate immediately afterward; if you have coagulated, dissolve it again soon after, and so forth. For the whole work is nothing other than **dissolve and coagulate** <note>original Latin: *solve, coagula*. This is the fundamental maxim of alchemy, representing the cyclic purification of matter.</note>. This is called acting quite contrary, playing the opposite game, and running backward.

See, I have again created a philosophical fog for you and thrown a cross-beam <note>An idiom for a "stumbling block" or intentional riddle.</note> in your path. Know, however, that coagulating is easier...

# Commentaries

Affairs and the restless **war of priests** <note>original German: *Pfaffenkrieg*; refers to the endless theological and sectarian disputes common during the Reformation era</note>, which never takes an end so long as the **coarse blockheads** <note>original German: *grobe Höltzlen*; literally "coarse little woods," a pejorative term for ignorant or stubborn people</note> live upon the earth. These things we shall now let pass.

But if one wishes to come to the knowledge of our intended **Secret** <note>original Latin: *Secrets*</note> and not be deceived, but rather reach the very foundation, let him steer clear of bad books and read the Holy Scripture—that is, the true **Philosophers** <note>original Latin: *Philosophos*; here referring to the ancient alchemical masters who were seen as divinely inspired</note> themselves. Let him hold to and pay attention to their **concordance** <note>original Latin: *Concordantz*; the underlying agreement or harmony between different authorities</note> and believe simply where they agree. Among other things, they testify with one voice concerning the course of Nature, her materials, and the **operations** <note>original Latin: *operationibus*; the chemical or natural processes</note> she carries out beneath the earth.

Think for yourself on what Nature makes the **Metals** <note>original Latin: *Metalla*</note> from; it is not fitting for me to speak further. You would gladly approach the **furnace** <note>original German: *Heintzen*; likely referring to the "Lazy Heinz" or Athanor, a self-feeding furnace used by alchemists</note>; look where those **spirits** <note>original Latin: *Spiritus*; refers to subtle vapors or the volatile "essence" of substances</note> run which give gold and silver, whether they are found in **liquid** <note>original Latin: *liquida*</note> or **solid form** <note>original Latin: *solida forma*</note>. Collect a small vial full of them and plug it well at the top. Only take care that no evil spirit comes to you and misleads you by night, for it is quite dark in the depths of the mountain. You must use your own light, as all those must who wish to enter the mountain <note>The author uses mining as a metaphor for alchemical exploration, where the "mountain" represents the hidden interior of matter</note>, where each has a special light hanging from his thumb. Observe where the apple or pear is present, and to which place it falls. There it remains. Therefore it is said: **Either this or something similar** <note>original Latin: *Aut hoc aut simile*; a common alchemical phrase suggesting that the exact substance may vary, but its nature must be the same</note>. There it remains again, and much more besides.

### Concerning the Little Peasant

Folio 7. If he wishes to comprehend the whole work briefly and pay close attention, etc.

Firstly, regarding the **subject matter** <note>original Latin: *subjectum*; in alchemy, this refers to the "prime matter" or the starting substance of the Great Work</note>, Nature—for the birth of metals within the crevices and veins of the mountains—and the **Philosophers** <note>original Latin: *Philosophi*; referring to the ancient alchemical masters</note>—for the preparation of their Stone outside the mountains—have the same one material. This material proves itself equal in power and might, performing its task for the **Philosopher** <note>original Latin: *Philosopho*</note> just as well as for Nature. For when there are identical **materials** <note>original Latin: *Materialia*</note>, an identical furnace, identical fire, and identical **sublimation** <note>original Latin: *Sublimation*; the process of heating a substance until it vaporizes and then condenses back into a solid</note>, **operation** <note>original Latin: *Operation*</note>, and effect, then necessarily one and the same work must result.

For the artist follows Nature's lead and adheres to her process, except that in all respects he knows how to improve, correct, and ennoble Nature. In this case, he is therefore above Nature and a master of Nature, for he carries out his work from Nature’s foundation much further than Nature herself, who in many respects cannot help herself. The power indeed lies within her, but she often cannot execute it because she lacks **reason** <note>original Latin: *Ration*; the intellectual capacity to direct natural forces</note>; for you have never heard that Nature ever gave birth to the **Philosophers' Stone** <note>original Latin: *Lapidem Philosophorum*</note> or the **form of gold** <note>original Latin: *formam auri*</note> on her own. Therefore, so that all things may be well-ordered, the human will must mix with Nature. And where one might wish to destroy the other, the human will must intervene and still the quarrel, so that peace and unity may be maintained.

<summary>This page explains that the alchemist and Nature use the same raw materials, but argues that the "Artist" is superior because they possess the reason necessary to perfect and ennoble these materials into the Philosophers' Stone.</summary>

### Commentaria

Folio 7.

The business and restless war of the priests <note>original German: *Pfaffenkrieg*; refers to the ongoing theological and academic disputes among the clergy and scholars of the time</note>, which never takes an end so long as the coarse blockheads <note>original German: *grobe Höltzlen*; literally "coarse little woods," a derogatory term for stubborn or unrefined people</note> live upon the earth. These we shall now let pass.

But if one wishes to arrive at the knowledge of our intended secret and not be deceived, but rather reach the very foundation, let him avoid bad books and read the Divine Scripture—that is, the true **Philosophers** themselves. Let him hold to and pay attention to their **concordance** <note>original German: *Concordantz*; the points where different alchemical authorities agree despite their cryptic language</note>, and believe simply where they harmonize. These testify, among other things, with a unanimous voice concerning the course of **Nature**, her **materials**, and her **operations** <note>original Latin: *operationibus*; the chemical or natural processes</note> which she carries out beneath the earth.

But as for what **Nature** makes **metals** from—ponder that yourself; it is not fitting for me to speak further. You would like to approach the **Heinz** <note>original: *Heintzen*; likely referring to the "Lazy Heinz" or Athanor, a specialized furnace designed to maintain a constant heat for long periods without constant supervision</note>. Look where those same **spirits** <note>original Latin: *spiritus*; the volatile essences or vapors within the earth</note> run that give **gold** and **silver**, whether they are found in liquid or solid form. Collect a small flask full of them and seal the top well. Only take care that no evil spirit comes to you to lead you astray at night, for it is quite dark in the depths of the **mountain**. You must use a narrow light, as is necessary for all who wish to enter the mountain, where each one has a special light hanging from his thumb <note>a reference to the *Grubenlicht* or miner's candle, which was traditionally attached to the thumb to keep the hands free for climbing and tools</note>. Consider where the apple or pear is present, and where or to what place it falls. There it remains. Therefore it is said: *Either this or something similar* <note>original Latin: *Aut hoc aut simile*</note>. There it remains again, and much more besides.

## Fol. 7. If he wishes to understand the whole work briefly and be attentive, etc.

Firstly, regarding the <term>subject matter <note>original Latin: *subjectum*; refers to the primary material or "first matter" used to begin the alchemical work</note></term>, Nature—in the birthing of metals within the crevices and veins of the mountains—and the <term>Philosophers <note>original Latin: *Philosophi*; the ancient masters of alchemy</note></term>—in preparing their Stone outside of the mountains—both employ the same material. This material proves itself equal in both power and might. Indeed, things go as well for the <term>Philosopher</term> as they do for Nature. For when the same <term>materials <note>original Latin: *materialia*</note></term>, the same furnace, the same fire, the same <term>sublimation <note>original Latin: *sublimatio*; the process of purifying a substance by heating it into vapor</note></term>, <term>operation <note>original Latin: *operatio*</note></term>, and effect are present, then necessarily the same work must result from them.

For the <term>Artist <note>original Latin: *artista*; the practicing alchemist</note></term> imitates Nature and follows her <term>process <note>original Latin: *processus*</note></term>, except that he knows how to improve it in every part: to <term>correct <note>original Latin: *corrigere*</note></term> and to ennoble Nature. In this regard, he is above Nature and a Master of Nature; for he carries out his work from the <term>foundation <note>original Latin: *fundamentum*</note></term> of Nature to a much higher degree than Nature herself, who in many respects cannot help herself. The power is certainly within her, but she often lacks the means to carry it out because she lacks <term>Reason <note>original Latin: *ratio*; the guiding intelligence or logic required to perfect a process</note></term>. For you have never heard of Nature ever giving birth to the <term>Philosopher's Stone <note>original Latin: *lapidem philosophorum*</note></term> or the <term>form of gold <note>original Latin: *formam auri*; the perfected essence of the metal</note></term> on her own. Therefore, so that all things may be properly accomplished, the Will of Man must mix with Nature. And should one part wish to obstruct the other, the Artist must step in and settle the quarrel, so that peace and unity may be maintained.

**subject** <note>the primary material of the alchemical work</note> a **Vital Spirit** <note>original Latin: *Spiritus Vitalis*; the life-giving force believed to animate all living things</note> / of which we have heard above / in which all living and growing things on Earth participate / how would it then not also propagate itself / and have growth from within itself? ### Concerning the Little Farmer.

When green wood or a branch contains an unspoiled seed, what honest and abundant growth <note>original: *Wucher*; in this historical context, it refers to natural increase or multiplication rather than the modern sense of usury</note> can be achieved with it, if one allows its rights and necessities to be fulfilled. He <note>referring to the "Little Farmer," an allegorical figure for the skilled alchemist</note> knows what creatures are capable of, those which still possess their inner hidden power, compared to dry wood or those things that are dead and barren. When he either casts all kinds of seeds into the ground, or grafts branches onto a wild trunk, cultivates the noble grapevine and produces little roots <term>little roots</term> <note>original: *Würtzlein*; the foundational strength or rootlets of a plant</note>, clears the hedges and lays them low, prepares the fields and gardens, and undertakes such work, he then experiences and knows where profit is made; and conversely, where all applied effort and labor is in vain, undertaken with loss and waste of time. Therefore, he also wants nothing to do with other materials <note>original Latin: *materialibus*</note> that do not possess this greenness within them.

Beware of the deceased bodies <note>original Latin: *Corporibus*</note> and the stones that are dead, says a philosopher <note>original Latin: *Philosophus*</note>, for in them there is no path. Our seed has such power that it can not only raise itself again from the grave after putrefaction <term>putrefaction</term> <note>original Latin: *putrefaction*; the essential alchemical stage of decay and blackening, believed to be the necessary precursor to rebirth and purification</note> and make itself alive, but can also—which is wondrous to hear—give life to that which is dead and has never had life within itself, and direct that which is corrupted into growth.

the eggs are only fostered <note>original: *foviert*; from the Latin *fovere*, meaning to cherish or keep warm</note> and given natural warmth. Let that same warmth come from wherever it may; one could stick the eggs into horse manure <term>horse manure: a common alchemical heat source, as decomposing manure provides a steady, gentle "digestive" temperature</term> or a bake-oven, and place them there in dry and crushed chicken manure or other dust, and provide the proper heat, and the same result will be achieved. The philosophers <note>Meaning the alchemists or natural scientists of the era.</note> do not argue about the external fire, except that it must be in accordance with nature.

Instead, a single man and a peasant alone raises twenty thousand at once; yes, in various ovens shaped almost like our bake-ovens, he hatches a hundred thousand eggs in one house. He does nothing else but attend to them day and night with natural warmth, placing and sticking these eggs inside the ovens into the rubbed-down chicken or camel manure, one next to the other. The peasants in Egypt practice this; yet our Masters <note>original: *Magistri*; referring to university-educated scholars</note>, who have studied for 20 or 30 years, would likely consider it an impossible fable.

I am amazed that the Germans—who otherwise, like apes, imitate everything (though they are also inventors of many stately works)—do not also put such a craft <note>original: *artificium*</note> into practice. They could, given the opportunity and other requirements, have and manage it just as well as those people; and it only requires one man to make a beginning of the matter among us.

...shown <note>original: *wiesen haben*; this completes the thought from the previous page: "shown it to be possible."</note>. This bird originally came from Arabia, as they say, or had its dwelling in those parts, but now—praise God—it is also found in our own lands. I believe it departed from those places and came up to us with the storks in Egypt, after the Arabs became such a predatory people.

The ancients have unanimously and consistently given witness to this **Phoenix**. I wish to set down here the words with which a learned and industrious man recently summarized this bird's kind and wondrous nature, and its whole manner of being, in brief. Namely, how it first burns itself, suffocates, and turns to ash; from which ash afterwards, through **rebirth**, a new **Phoenix** bird—in all respects identical to the previous one—springs forth and rises. Thus it moves itself, kills itself, brings itself back to life, and thereby rejuvenates itself and preserves its race without the help or intervention of any other, but rather possesses within itself both the **active agent** <term>active agent: original: *agens*; the force that acts or causes change</term> and the **passive subject** <term>passive subject: original: *patiens*; the matter that is acted upon or undergoes change</term>. His words are:

**Another Anonymous [Author]** <note>original Latin: *Alius Anonymus*</note>. # Regarding the Little Peasant.

...is, and is found before the composition <note>original Latin: *ante compositionem*</note>, which the aforementioned author brings up in his little book and insists upon, claiming it costs no small amount. But I fear that even if he had many thousands of florins <term>gulden: a gold coin common in the Holy Roman Empire; here the author uses it to signify great wealth</term> in hand, he would still find it difficult to buy—indeed, he would never even catch sight of it—unless he were "beaked" differently <note>original German: *geschnäbelt*; an idiomatic expression likely meaning to be taught a different lesson or to have one's perspective corrected</note>. Further.

**Morienus** <note>a legendary 7th-century hermit and alchemist</note>, a good ancient author: "Everything that is bought at a great price is false and useless" <note>original Latin: *Omnis res, quę magno emitur precio, mendax est & inutilis*</note>. Listen to what this means: Add the minor premise: "Gold is bought at a great price" <note>original Latin: *Aurum magno emitur precio*</note>. From this, make the conclusion yourself—and then see how the opposing opinion <note>original Latin: *adversa sententia*</note> holds up.

**Arnoldus** <note>referring to Arnaldus de Villa Nova, a prominent 13th-century physician and alchemist</note>: "Hold firmly that the expenses of our most noble art do not exceed the price of two gold coins <note>original Latin: *duorum aureorum*</note> in its first purchase—that is, in its operation" <note>original Latin: *Firmiter teneas, quòd expensæ nostræ nobilissimæ artis, non excedunt precium duorum aureorum, in prima suâ emptione, id est, operatione*</note>.

**Geber** <note>the Latinized name of Jabir ibn Hayyan, the "Father of Chemistry"</note>: "If in the work you lose your money <note>original Latin: *æs tuum*: literally "your copper," often used to mean base money or wealth</note>, do not unjustly attack us, but blame your own imprudence; for our science does not require great expenses" <note>original Latin: *Si in operando æs tuum amiseris, nos non iniquè corrodas, sed tuæ imputes imprudentiæ: Scientia enim nostra magnas non requirit impensas*</note>.

And again **Geber**: "It is not necessary to consume your wealth, because for a low price, if you have not been ignorant of the principles of the art, you will achieve your purpose" <note>original Latin: *Non oportet tua bona consumere, quia vili precio, Si artis principia non ignoraveris, propositum consequéris*</note>.

For since there are people here from all three sides of the world <note>Likely referring to the three known continents: Europe, Asia, and Africa.</note>, you may well consider that the customs of the land, the era, and the <term>intellects</term> <note>original: *Ingenia*; plural of *Ingenium*, referring to the varied minds of men.</note> cannot all match perfectly, even if they agree in describing a matter and its foundation and maintain <term>concordance</term> <note>original: *Concordantz*; a state of agreement or harmony between different texts or ideas.</note>.

### Folio 8. Furthermore, you should also be understanding, etc.

All creatures on Earth are divided into three kingdoms, three lineages, or types of created bodies, which are distinct from one another: namely, that they are either vegetable <note>original: *Vegetabilisch*; referring to plants and growing things.</note>, or animal <note>original: *Animalisch*</note>, or mineral <note>original: *Mineralisch*</note>.

One must also not seek it among the animal creatures, such as all kinds of beasts, humans, cattle, birds, fish, or worms, or anything that comes from these; all such things are unsuitable. ...simply let them remain, and not mix the three types and lineages of these earthly things with one another, but rather maintain that same natural distinction and let every creature follow its own course and remain in its kingdom, according to the order of God. It has secrets at the back and at the front, and there are also secrets hidden in the middle.

And who would be so desperate as to direct the **dreadful curses** <note>original: *diras Execrationes*</note> of all pious and sensible men upon his own head? Such a person might name it. # ON GENERATION <note>original Latin: *DE GENERATIONE*</note>
## Of Metals <note>original Latin: *Metallorum*</note>

All <term>Philosophers <note>in this context, "Philosophers" refers to alchemists and natural scientists</note></term> who have described the generation and birth of metals agree unanimously in this: that all metals originate and take their beginning from two things, namely from **Sulfur** <note>original: *Sulphure*</note> and **Mercury** <note>original: *Mercurio*</note>. Mercury is their Body and <term>Subject <note>original Latin: *Subjectum*; the underlying substance or matter that receives a form</note></term>. This is seen and proven not only by visual evidence when they are in <term>flux <note>original: *Fluß*; the molten or liquid state of metal</note></term>—into which they could otherwise never be brought—but also from experience. For one can extract from all metals, from each and every one, its own "running" <note>liquid</note> mercury and release it from its sulfur. ### Commentaries

Tinctures are pure **forms**; but in metals, there is less **sulfur** <term>original: *Sulphur*; the active, combustible principle or "soul" of a metal</term>—namely, only as much as that specific metal requires for its **perfection** <note>In alchemical theory, every metal strives toward the "perfection" of gold; "perfection" here refers to the specific balance of principles that defines a metal's identity</note>. Thus, if such a **Sulfur of Venus** <note>Copper sulfur</note> also takes possession of the **Body of the Moon** <note>the physical substance of silver</note>, it overshadows the **Sulfur of the Moon** and brings the lunar sulfur under its control, or casts it aside and removes it, thereby transforming the **Mercury of the Moon** <note>the metallic principle within silver</note> into **copper**.

For if one can extract the tincture from the **Sun** <note>Gold</note> using other common substances, so that a white body remains; or if one produces the **Mercury of the Sun**, as some laboratory workers do, and separates the white from the red: then one can certainly do so here much more effectively through powerful **tinctures**, to which everything must yield. There is, however, little profit in choosing to make copper or lead out of gold. But we are not here for the sake of profit, but for the sake of the **Art** <note>The "Art" refers to Alchemy, often called the "Great Art" (*Ars Magna*)</note>. He who possesses the Art can also create profit. Yet the Art is more excellent than money, gold, or silver—know this well. Therefore, because of the wonders of Nature and the Art, I have no doubt that some among the **philosophers** <note>Historical alchemists and natural scientists</note>, out of delight and for the sake of experimentation, experience, and knowledge, have prepared such things.

For it is just as great—indeed, a much greater Art in nature—to make copper out of gold as it is to make gold out of copper. One is accustomed to use **fermentation** <term>original: *fermentation*; the process of adding a small amount of a substance to "leaven" or transform a larger mass</term> to direct matters toward whichever end one desires.

# Commentaria

...and one be transformed into the other, and all of them finally **brought** into one.

In this, the philosophers have exerted themselves in many ways and have proven their masterpiece. For that fire should come from water, and again water from fire—do you not consider that a feat of art? In the *Turba* or Assembly of the Philosophers <note>original: *Turba Philosophorum*; one of the oldest and most influential Latin alchemical texts, written as a transcript of a debate between ancient sages</note>, it is written:

> Convert the elements, and you shall find what you seek. <note>original: *Converte elementa, & quod quæris, invenies*</note>

Regarding this, know that two elements are visible, namely Earth and Water; the other two elements, Fire and Air, are not seen. However, they are perceived and are contained within the former two. Once you have reconciled Mercury and Sulfur, Water and Earth with one another, you have then immediately turned the four elements into each other and brought them into one. But this does not happen as simply <note>original: *schlecht*; in this period, the word meant "simply" or "straightforwardly" rather than "poorly"</note> as you might think; rather, you must be a good physicist <note>original: *physicus*; a student of nature or natural philosopher</note> and know how to arrange a skillful and intertwined **circulation** <term>original: *Circulation*; the alchemical process where a substance is heated so it rises as vapor, condenses, and falls back down, mimicking the natural cycle of rain and evaporation</term> here, so that those parts which are diametrically opposed <note>original: *ex diametro*</note> and to the highest degree contrary to one another are reconciled and made one through a subtle arrangement.

If one is to achieve the turning and reconciliation of the elements, one must investigate the qualities <note>original: *qualitates*</note> of the elements and take them up one after the other, dealing with the matter in an entirely orderly fashion, as Nature permits and gives you the reins <note>original: *den Zaum verhengen*; an idiom meaning to slacken the reins or allow the natural course of things to take over</note>. For every single element has two qualities within it. Earth is dry and cold; Water is moist and cold; Air is moist and warm; the

->### About the Little Peasant <note>original: *vber den kleinen Bawren*; likely a commentary on "The Little Peasant," a work attributed to the alchemist Johann Grasshoff</note><-

Fire is dry and warm. Thus, the aforementioned elements are, on one side, contrary to one another in their qualities and innate properties, and are diametrically <note>original: *ex diametro*</note> opposed. On the other side, however, they communicate with each other, and one agrees and shares a likeness with another. Thus they hang together in an intertwined way, as if on a chain.

So one must not proceed here impetuously, but rather act reasonably and proceed in an orderly fashion. One must bring the contrary elements <term>original: *elementa*; the four basic building blocks of matter: Fire, Air, Water, and Earth</term> together on that side where they resemble each other in quality and can tolerate one another, so that the others may also follow afterward, and each is transposed into the other in an intertwined manner. This continues until all four are thoroughly changed, one transformed into the other, and finally they become entirely equal and one, in order to prepare the philosopher's stone <note>original: *lapidem philosophorum*; the legendary substance capable of turning base metals into gold and granting eternal life</note>. 

Now, this is the secret: Earth and Fire meet one another in dryness; Water and Air meet one another in moisture. Because of these shared qualities, there would be no difficulty, and they would soon become one with each other, for they have a ladder and a handle between them. But for Fire and Water, or Earth and Air, to be turned into one another—that is difficult. It would be impossible if such a thing were not done with the greatest reason <note>original: *cum summa ratione*</note>, and if Fire were not first transformed into Air, and Earth into Water. By means of these matching qualities, the extremes <note>original: *extrema*</note> are brought together, each turned into the other, and finally thus reconciled.

And all of this occurs during the period of ripening through gentle cooking <note>original: *suavi decoctione*</note>, during which the alchemist <note>original: *Artist*</note> must not work against nature with too much heat while separating the qualities of the elements, until he reaches the fourth degree and has completed the entire circle of transformations. As for how to actually put this into practice: reflect upon it yourself and read what the philosophers have written on the subject; one should not spoon-feed <note>original: *Muß einstreichen*; literally "to smear porridge," an idiom meaning to make things too easy or provide every detail without effort</note> everything to a person.

The summary of it is this: You must turn Water into Earth, and Earth into Water (just as has occurred in the case of common mercury <note>original: *Mercurio*</note>). This is done through specific means and methods, as mentioned: namely through purification, through digestion <term>original: *digestion*; a process where substances are softened and matured by gentle, steady heat over a long period</term>, and the introduction and balancing of the qualities of the elements. For the Moist <note>original: *Humidum*</note> is gradually and successively <note>original: *successive*</note> balanced with the Dry <note>original: *Sicco*</note>, and the Dry <note>original: *Siccum*</note> with the Moist <note>original: *Humido*</note>. Each is incorporated and united with the other through cooking <note>original: *per decoctionem*</note> so that one takes on the nature and quality of the other. Finally, they leave behind their own individual natures, surrender themselves entirely to one another, mix together, and constitute a unique essence <note>original: *besonders Wesen*</note>.

## Commentaria

...extraction / is not only for the sake of its purity: But in that it is thus extracted / circulated / and turned one into the other / and a general equality is achieved among them / finally / by means of the cooking and long **digestion** <note>original: *digestion*; the alchemical process of subjecting a substance to gentle, continuous heat to mature it</note> / a general **essence** <note>original: *Essents*</note> of all elements comes from it / which is / as it were / a **common form of all elements** <note>original: *communis forma omnium elementorum*</note> / a subtle, artistic extract of the elements / which / whereas the common elements are changeable and destructible / just as they likewise make their **bodies** <note>original: *corpora*</note> destructible / especially on account of **inequality** <note>original: *unæqualitet*; referring to a lack of balance between the elemental forces</note>. ### Commentaries

The first means by which one unites and brings together **Man** and **Wife**—the **Sulfur** <note>original: *Sulphur*; in alchemy, the active, masculine, and combustible principle</note> and **Mercury** <note>original: *Mercurium*; the passive, feminine, and volatile principle</note>—is that they approach each other in friendship and with gentleness. Through reasonable **cohabitation** <note>original: *beywohnung*; a metaphor for the chemical combination of substances</note>, which requires a considerable amount of time, they should win each other over and create peace.

But if the proposed means are tried and applied to the "evil wife," and she still does not surrender, but despite all the effort expended, she persists in even greater displeasure—becoming fickle, unstable, frivolous, unruly, proud, and arrogant—as is the custom with some women who, once the husband has brought them to honor and they have become magnificent, prove themselves rebellious and spoiled, wanting to abandon the husband and depart.

If the husband does not wish to be stripped of his status but rather remain in his domestic honors, he must find means to bind <note>original: *banne*; in an alchemical sense, to "fix" a volatile substance so it does not evaporate</note> and humble her. And so it is likely to go with our **Mercury** and **Sulfur**. This has occurred to many a practitioner who was unable to help himself due to lack of understanding and faintheartedness, because he was not courageous enough, as a **Philosopher** <note>original: *Philosophus*; a term for an alchemical authority or adept</note> says in one place:

> I saw in our time a certain man who knew the **elements** <note>original: *elementa*</note>, just as I did. Then, through his efforts, he established this arrangement; but he did not reach the joy of it, because of his own gloominess in governing the process, his powerlessness, and his excessive haste. <note>original: *Vidi tempore nostro quendam, qui elementa sciebat, quemadmodum & ego: Deinde medens hanc erexit dispositionem: Ad cujus letitiam non pervenit, propter tristitiam suam in regendo, & impotentiam, nimiamque festinationem*</note>

### About the Little Peasant

To the point <note>original: *ad propositum*</note>. Here our subtle Peasant <note>The "Little Peasant" is the namesake of this treatise, likely representing the practitioner or the primary material</note> observes that there are indeed means at hand which one must employ with **Mercury** <note>the volatile, "feminine" principle in alchemy</note> in case of necessity, by which one may humble this lewd woman (a **Philosopher** <note>an alchemical authority</note> calls her a "proud woman" <note>original Latin: *mulierem superbam*</note>) and bring her to obedience. This is done so that she—who always seeks to rule over the man, have the upper hand, lead him by the nose according to her whim, and even strip him of his domestic honors—may once again come under the power and hand of the man: so that she may go to meet her husband, and finally a balanced and permanent **marriage** <note>a stable chemical compound or the "Philosopher's Stone"</note> may come of it. For this is no matter for jesting; one must resist the evil in good time and not allow too much to proud, headstrong, and puffed-up women, nor permit them the **regiment** <note>rule or governance</note>, especially when it concerns land and people; they otherwise begin nothing good when they are the masters.

One writes of King **Ninus**, that he once permitted and handed over the government of his kingdom to his spouse, **Semiramis**, for two days: (I suspect it happened during a feast, when the wine had gone to his head and he had become merry.) She, the woman, accepted and took this up, and had her husband, **Ninus**, cast into prison; and she ruled not just for two days, but for some forty-odd years. And while she indeed accomplished many memorable things, she also committed great outrages. He should have reconsidered this handover...

For every <term>Spirit</term> <note>original: *Spiritus*</note> is volatile; if it is now to remain, it must be <term>fixed</term> <note>original: *figiert*</note>. But if it is to become fixed, this must happen by means of a Body—as you may well consider—by which it might be restrained. Now, there is no fixed Body other than <term>Gold</term> <note>original: *Sol*; symbolized by the Sun</note>, as is well known to everyone. Though they say that <term>Silver</term> <note>original: *Luna*; symbolized by the Moon</note> is also fixed, it is yet not so fixed, for when it burns upon the test or the cupel, it does lose something of itself.

Therefore, the <term>Philosophers</term> <note>original: *Philosophi*; referring to the traditional masters of alchemy</note> calcine only with the red body; and they also calcine the white with the red, which is a wondrous operation. Just as they then also ferment the white with the red, and similarly ferment the red beneath the white, it is once again a wondrous operation.

<summary>This page explains the necessity of adding a "fixed" body (like Gold) to volatile "spirits" to prevent them from evaporating during high-heat processes. It warns that without this fixation, the alchemist's work will be lost to the chimney as smoke.</summary>

One writes of <term>Alexander the Great</term> <note>original: "Alexandro Magno"</note> that during his <term>expedition</term> <note>original: "Peregrination"</note> he encountered the mighty King <term>Darius</term> and wished to be called a lord of that kingdom as well. He sent a message to the approaching <term>Darius</term> to warn him off, saying that he [Darius] would achieve nothing with his few people against such a mighty and large crowd of innumerable folk that he [Alexander] commanded. Along with this, he sent him a sack full of <term>poppy seed</term> <note>original: "Magsaat"</note> with the message that if he could count these little seeds, then he would also be able to count <term>Darius’s</term> people.

But Alexander sent him back a single peppercorn in return and had him told: This single little grain has more sharpness behind it than a whole sack full of his <term>rapeseed</term> <note>original: "Rubsaamens"</note>.

Darius eventually learned the truth of this. For Alexander fought him with thirty thousand men and cast down all his power—he who had believed there was no end to his people. Therefore, it does not depend on the multitude or the large crowd, but rather on the power and virtue which is concentrated in small <term>bodies</term> <note>original: "Corporibus"</note> and driven into a narrow space; for this reason, they are all the stronger and more furious. Whereas power in large things is scattered, for which reason they are also that much weaker.

Therefore, with a little <term>saffron</term> <note>original: "Saffran"</note> you can color a whole vessel full of water; with a little poison infect a large goblet; and with a small <term>quantity</term> of <term>leaven</term> <note>original: "Sawrteyg"; here used as an alchemical metaphor for the "Ferment" or the Stone</note> infect a great mass of <term>Mercury</term> <note>original: "Mercurij"</note>; and with a tiny little fire burn a whole mountain, if it were combustible.

The aforementioned natural proportion must also be maintained with our **Mercury** <note>original: "Mercurio"; representing the fluid, feminine principle in alchemy.</note> and **Sulfur** <note>original: "Sulphure"; representing the fiery, masculine principle.</note>, and one must know the power and the nature of both **ingredients** <note>original: "Ingredientium"</note>, and arrange both **weights** <note>original: "pondera"</note> **according to physical proportion** <note>original: "secundum proportionem physicam"</note>; for a good portion of Sulfur allows itself to be **blessed** <note>original: "seeligen"; here meaning to be fixed, perfected, or brought to a state of alchemical "salvation" or stability.</note> with a small portion of the **Soul of the Sun** <note>original: "Animæ solis"; the spiritual essence or "tincture" of gold.</note>: and it is required in every way that one establishes it thus.

->### On the Little Peasant <note>original: "vber den kleinen Bawren"; a reference to the work of Johann Grasshoff, a famous alchemical author</note><-

...join and unite them together? You would have to catch the **fore-run** <term>fore-run: the first, most volatile portion of a liquid to emerge during distillation</term> in a separate glass until the other part gradually follows after; only then can you conjoin them and bring them into one. As distillers <term>distillers: specialists in the extraction of spirits</term> and apothecaries <term>apothecaries: early pharmacists</term> sometimes do with herbs and flowers which do not bloom or appear at the same time; yet because they wish to have the water and **essence** <note>original: "Essenz"; the concentrated "soul" or medicinal power of a plant</note> of both together, they distill one and keep it well sealed until they produce the other, and then they mix them.

Or even the **alchemists**, when they wish to make **strong waters** <note>original: "starcke Wasser"; typically corrosive acids like nitric acid or aqua regia</note> for their **solutions** <note>original: "solutionibus"; the process of dissolving solids into liquids</note>, and the **materials** <note>original: "materialia"</note> will not tolerate each other in the **retort** <term>retort: a glass vessel with a long, curved neck used for distilling substances</term>, but rather strike against each other because they are of opposing natures; thus they distill one after the other and pour them together afterward, which is said to be just as effective as if they had been drawn over together and at once.

In this case, however, it is not at all appropriate, but rather carries danger, and such a thing is impossible to do; for once they are separated from one another, they will never again accept each other.

Therefore take note. # Concerning the Little Peasant
<note>The "Little Peasant" (*der kleine Bauer*) refers to a famous 16th-century alchemical treatise often attributed to Johann Grasshoff.</note>

No **body** <term>body: the physical or solid aspect of a substance before it is spiritualized</term> enters into another, nor is it truly and fundamentally <note>original: "in radice," meaning "at the root"</note> united with it. Nature, when one allows a gentle and pleasant warmth to befall her, does and completes for herself everything that is necessary for the equipping of a <term>created being</term> <note>original Latin: "Creati"</note>, or the introduction of a new form. ### Commentaries

The second **Virtue and Power** is the **Retentive and Coagulative Nature** <note>original Latin: "Natura retentiva & coagulativa"</note>. For Nature does not only bring to herself that which is useful and helpful for her continuation—provided she is not hindered by a lack of what she desires or otherwise—but she also possesses within herself the bonds with which she may hold and place in fetters that which she draws and brings to herself. Indeed, she transforms the same within herself (while in the meantime she selects the purest parts, rejects the remainder, and brings them to the exit <note>referring to the excretion of waste or impurities</note>) and causes them to grow.

And here she requires no other <term>calcination</term> <note>the process of reducing a substance to a powder through high heat</note> or <term>fixation</term> <note>the alchemical process of making a volatile substance stable or "fixed" so it no longer evaporates</note>. **Nature retains nature** <note>original Latin: "Natura naturam retinet," a fundamental alchemical axiom suggesting that like substances act upon one another</note>, and such skill is caused by and originates from dryness, where the cold **constricts** <note>original: "Constringiert"</note> the corrupted and uniform parts and impresses them into the **earth** <note>original Latin: "terræ"</note>.

The third **Power of Nature in generating and increasing things** <note>original Latin: "Potentia naturæ, in rebus generandis & augmentandis"</note> is the **Digestive Virtue, which occurs through putrefaction, or within putrefaction** <note>original Latin: "Virtus Digestiva, quæ fit per putrefactionem, seu in putrefactione"</note>, in moderate and tempered heat and moisture. There, Nature digests, transforms, and introduces another kind and quality; she makes the raw refined, the bitter sweet, the hard soft, the harsh mild, the rough gentle, and the unseasonable and wild domestic. What was initially unfit, she now makes skillful and capable, and promotes it toward the final execution and perfection of the intended Work, presenting the **Ingredients** <note>original Latin: "Ingredientia"</note> for the **Composition** <note>original Latin: "Composition"</note>.

The fourth **Power of Nature** is the **Expulsive Virtue** <note>original Latin: "Virtus expulsi-"</note>

# On the Little Peasant
<note>The "Little Peasant" refers to *Der kleine Bauer*, a famous alchemical text often attributed to Johann Grasshoff which uses the metaphor of farming to explain chemical processes.</note>

...remain in balance with the natural moisture and be able to perform their office. This fire or heat—as soon as the human or animal <note>original German: *Thür*, an archaic spelling of *Tier*</note> dies, and life is taken from them perhaps by an accident, be it through unnatural diseases or from the outside in some other way—the heat also departs from them immediately, and the animal becomes cold. Or otherwise, the heat leaves when death occurs naturally (for not only the occurring external accidents, but also all other diseases are something violent <note>original Latin: *Violentum quid*</note>) and the fire within them is extinguished before they die, upon which death must follow once again.

Likewise, to speak of the third kingdom of nature, in all metals and minerals there also lies a heat. These mineral bodies <note>original Latin: *Corpora*</note> just as well—and even much more—have an inner hidden fire within them, which nevertheless does not show, reveal, or allow itself to be felt in such a way as in other animals, nor even as in growing things. But it is no less strong and powerful. One becomes aware and perceives this when one anatomizes <term>anatomizes: to "anatomize" a mineral in alchemy means to chemically deconstruct it to reveal its internal essence or "spirit."</term> that same mineral, searches its nature and internal parts, and brings forth what is hidden in it, letting the experiment speak.

Thus, there is nothing among all the species of nature, in all three of its kingdoms, which does not have its own internal fire. By this, it is driven and moved, and its life is maintained and propagated.

### Commentaries

Our *Subject* <note>original: *Subjectum*; in alchemy, this refers to the base material or "prime matter" chosen for the chemical process.</note> also has a fire; and among creatures and minerals, it is not the least or weakest fire within itself. It has hidden within it the most wonderfully powerful fire, compared to which common external elemental fire <note>the ordinary fire found in a hearth or furnace.</note> is to be regarded as water. For no elemental fire, no matter how strong it may be, can consume or destroy gold—which is the most stable substance in fire among all bodies—that is, to strip it of its essence. But our fire and our water, they alone can do it.

This fire, when it was recovered after seventy years during the redemption and return of the Jews to *Jerusalem* by the descendants of the wise ancient priests, had meanwhile *transformed* <note>original: *resolviert*, meaning dissolved or changed state.</note> within the mountain and become a thickened water. Such fire, however, sleeps in our *Subject*, is entirely still and quiet, without any action...

# Commentary

The first is the external fire, which the keeper brings forth, which we call the <term>hearth fire</term> <note>Latin: *ignem focalem*; the literal fire in the furnace</note>, to which wood is added—such as that brought from the Black Forest—which is the primary matter we have at hand to discuss. ### Commentaries

Furthermore, <term>homogeneity</term> <note>original: *Homogeneitas*; a state where all parts are of the same nature</note> consists of nothing but the most noble, pure, and penetrable parts (which constitute the whole). Finally, this purity is acquired through <term>decoction</term> <note>the process of heating or boiling a substance to extract its essence</note> and a slow, hidden, gentle, and continuous motion: in which there is a power that separates and connects. And by this means, this Matter is prepared for perpetuity, being henceforth subject to no corruption or destruction. If these things are properly cared for by the skill of the <term>Artificer</term> <note>original: *Artificis*; the alchemist or craftsman</note>, there is nothing now to prevent Nature—which fails in nothing and admits no error—from attaining its best and most perfect end.

If in the summer, during the growing and <term>ripening</term> <note>original: *zeittigũg*; the process of coming to maturity</note> of all fruits and other plants, you did not want to leave Nature to her natural and easy course with her lovely and pleasant summer heat or warmth: but instead wanted to strengthen the external heat and sunshine for the plants—giving the apple tree, grapevine, or herb even more heat by adding glowing coals or flaming fire, and thus trying to "strengthen" Nature through this and be helpful to her in her works, wanting to shorten the time of ripening so that you might have your <term>harvest</term> <note>original: *Herbst*; literally "Autumn," but used here for the harvest time</note> sooner, or have your wine riper and earlier: that would indeed be a foolish undertaking. Such an action and applied labor would in no way help, but rather hinder, or completely burn out the natural sap, and bring everything to ruin.

# concerning the Little Farmer.

So too in the animal realm: if you wished to cast more fire upon the natural warmth of the stomach, as well as the entire human body, and overwhelm it with many spices which also come from India, or as some have the custom, to assist it with daily pepper and strongly seasoned foods—thinking thereby to strengthen the natural warmth of man and the stomach—he acts, in my opinion, foolishly, and only makes himself colder through this.
