## Commentary

...[Stone] of the **Philosophers** <note>original Latin: *Philosophorum*</note> is once made and brought to its end, though the alchemist may have ever so little of it, he nonetheless possesses an infinite treasure that cannot run out or drain away from him. No **potentate's** <note>A monarch or powerful ruler</note> treasure of gold and silver is so great that it might not be lost, weakened, or completely brought to nothing through spending. A **Philosopher** <note>An alchemist or practitioner of the "natural philosophy"</note> however, need have no such worry, no matter how great and excessive his expenditure might be. [Unless] he should wish to take no care for his affairs at all and cast aside all human affection—which is impossible for such a man. For **by way of augmentation** <note>original Latin: *per modum augmentationis*—the process of increasing the quantity and potency of the Stone</note>, starting from a small beginning, he can soon reach and maintain a significant weight of the substance, as much as he wants and as often as he wants. 

Thus, it is not necessary to return to the very beginning of the **operation** <note>The "Great Work" or the multi-stage alchemical process</note> whenever his **Stone** <term>Lapis: the Philosopher's Stone</term> has been nearly exhausted through **Projection** <term>Projection: the final stage of alchemy where a small amount of the Stone is "projected" onto molten base metal to transmute it into gold or silver</term>. He need not act like someone who has worn out a garment and must buy new material, spending time and labor once again until the tailor has finished it, and dedicating a period of nine, ten, twelve months, or even one or two years as he did before. Rather, one needs only to add a small portion of the completed **Stone** <note>original Latin: *Lapidis*</note> to a part of its initial natural **Liquor** <term>Liquor: the "water" or solvent used at the start of the work, often called "mercurial water"</term> or companion water. One must then enclose such a **Composition** <note>original Latin: *Compositum*</note> in the glass and command the heat, giving each appearance its proper degree...

...therefore one person can fare well / while the other suffers lack. For that which this one possesses / has brought under his control / and holds in his hands / the other must do without / and remain in want / and be so much the poorer: This is because no more fields are available or can be found within the jurisdiction and district where the community has gathered than those that have already been measured out. And those who possess many goods and estates do not wish to enter into any communal sharing with the others / but rather hold fast to "mine and thine" <note>original Latin: *meum und tuum*</note>. Now, the larger the portion or piece that one person claims for himself—whether through reckless grabbing or foolish behavior <note>The original phrase "mit dem hengholzen und thorichten buben" likely refers to clumsy or unscrupulous ways of seizing land</note>—within that certain district / the smaller the portion the other must be satisfied with / to the point that he sometimes cannot even obtain what is necessary for his basic needs / while the other has an abundance. Thus, the fault here lies not with "earth-usury" <term>Erdwucher: the natural, God-given increase of the soil</term> or with farming in itself <note>original Latin: *per se*</note> / but rather it brings about a burdensome "accident" <note>In this context, an "accident" refers to a negative side-effect or unintended consequence of an action</note> for the neighbor / caused by the one who conducts the business and takes up the farming.

In the industry of mining, one is spared these burdens and these occurring "accidents" / for there, no one does harm to another / nor does one person, out of greed and a desire to have much, seize too many of the landed estates / thereby withdrawing so much from the other and making his own heap larger. Moreover, it is in the interest of the Republic <note>original Latin: *Interest autem Reipub.*</note> that the common state / and the welfare of a land / people / city / or village be preserved among the inhabitants / and this should be done as much as is possible and feasible / so that through the start and increase of one person / the other is not oppressed / and so that he who is "down" may have the means to recover himself again / and all inequality and hindrances may be removed—

### On the Small Farmers

...do damage / but conduct their business outside the **surface** <note>original Latin: *superficie*</note> of this world / underground with the **little earth-men** <note>original German: *Erdmändlein*; small, gnome-like spirits traditionally believed to inhabit mines and guard treasures</note> / and travel toward the **center of the world** <note>original Latin: *Centro mundi*</note> / through the rock / with unbelievable labor: for they must strike through a whole / often nearly hard- and iron-like stone / wherever or to whichever side they wish / and wherever the vein of the mountain leads them. For know / that this sphere / upon which humans dwell / is a single stone / as all miners / and those who go down into the pits / have daily before their eyes. The soil, however, lies on the **surface of this globe** <note>original Latin: *superficie huius globi*</note> like a dust / upon this great stone (it is God’s **specimen-stone** <term>Handstein: Literally a "hand-stone," usually a beautiful mineral specimen kept in a collection, but here used to describe the entire Earth as a divine masterpiece</term>) all around it / in the thickness / which is necessary for the cultivation and preservation of all plants / and the fruits on the earth / for the benefit of mankind / and is ordained by God: and it was left behind by the **Great Flood** <note>original German: *sündfluß*</note> / which caused a noticeable inequality / and made a great wilderness within it / so that humans / foxes / bears / badgers / and rabbits may dig therein and conduct their business. For first / one commonly drives straight and on level ground at the side of the mountain / an **adit** <term>Stollen: A horizontal tunnel driven into a hillside for access or drainage in a mine</term> into the mountain through the **topsoil** <note>original German: *dammerd*</note> / for many **fathoms** <term>Klaffter: A historical unit of measurement, roughly the span of a man's outstretched arms or about 6 feet</term> long / where / so that the tunnel does not collapse / one must support it with timbering: Afterward / one comes upon the **unstable rock** <note>original German: *faulen berg*; literally "rotten mountain," referring to crumbly or soft strata that is dangerous to mine</note> / which one must likewise / as long as it lasts / provide with timbering. Finally one encounters the solid stone / which never gives way or changes / and seeks within it the **vein** <note>original German: *Gang*</note> / which alone carries the ore. After...

### Commentaries <note>original Latin: *Commentaria*</note>

...the vein along which the **miner** <term>Bergkman: A professional miner, often a status of significant technical skill in the early modern period</term> stretches himself. If this vein emerges into the light of day, so that one can see it and have good indications of its quality—through which **mountain range** <note>original German: *Gebürg*</note> and along which line it falls—then one drives a straight **adit** <term>Stolle: A horizontal passage leading into a mine for access or drainage</term> into the mountain and reaches the vein at the side, at the nearest point possible.

But if one does not know its **bearing** <note>original German: *stund*; literally "hour," referring to the direction on a mining compass</note>, or if it might have **faulted** <note>original German: *verworffen*; a geological displacement where the vein is cut off or shifted</note>, then one builds "into the cross" and enters **crosswise** <note>original German: *yberzwerch*</note> so that one does not miss it. For, since it is quite dark in the mountain and one cannot see well through the walls—as if looking through **spectacles** <note>original German: *Parillen*; an archaic term for eyeglasses</note>—one might otherwise continue to drive the adit right alongside the vein, or get further and further away from it, as I know by example has happened to some.

Upon such carelessness, however, depends the ruin of the **mine-owners** <term>Gwercken: The shareholders or investors who financed the mining operations and bore the financial risk</term>. For to build for a long time and encounter no **ore** <note>original German: *Erz*</note>, not yet to have reached the vein, or not to know it thoroughly, is the miner's greatest calamity.

But when one has a **noble vein** before him, which falls in its length through an entire mountain range (indeed, who knows if it does not go through the entire globe of this world and into the eternal depths, since one also finds mines on the other sides of the world?), then the miners should break into it immediately so that they may stir themselves upon it. The **hewers** <note>original German: *hewer*; the workers who physically cut the rock</note> on the aforementioned vein should, in all places—from behind and in front—sink shafts and drive tunnels upwards, and occupy the sites with workers, and thus hollow out an entire mountain. For it commonly happens that the deeper the work goes, the richer the ore reveals itself to be; but it also demands a greater cost for **hauling it up** <note>original German: *aufffördern*; the process of bringing ore and waste rock to the surface</note>.

# Regarding the Small-Scale Miner

...until you reach the lowest **strike** <term>Anbruch: the point where a mineral vein is first discovered or exposed</term>, so that you know what "traveling" <note>original: *fahren*; in historical mining terminology, this specifically means the act of descending into or moving through a mine</note> really means. Sometimes, because of the lack of air at such great depths, if one does not make a connection <term>Durchschlag: a tunnel that connects two different mine workings to allow air to circulate</term> with other neighboring **pits** <term>Gruben: mines</term>, or bring air from far behind through **ventilation pipes** <term>Lutten: wooden pipes or conduits used to funnel fresh air into deep mine shafts</term>, the mountain must be completely abandoned. One must say **"farewell"** <note>original: *Vale* (Latin)</note> to the strike, no matter how rich it may be.

In the midst of all this, these noble miners leave others—who outside the mine fight over worldly goods—undisturbed. They stretch themselves out beneath the mountain, each according to his own **working** <term>Baw: a specific area of excavation or a mining project</term>. Each calculates for himself the "nobility" <note>The author uses "nobility" here to refer to the purity or richness of the mineral vein.</note> of the **vein** <term>Gang: a mineral-bearing vein or lode</term> and trusts that he will strike **ore** <term>Erz</term>, for hope sustains almost all of them. 

And so they have their workshop and tireless labor within the mountain. # Regarding the Small-Scale Miner

These letters were entrusted to the **Sun** to carry there, who, as a faithful and ready messenger, has allowed itself to be used to deliver both the writing and the reply confidentially to both parties every day within twenty-four hours.

However, those good people [the Antipodeans] may be warned by the written reports of some of our people—which always arrive safely via the aforementioned messenger [the Sun]—and also by the messenger's own verbal testimony. For the Sun daily witnesses the countless evil dealings that occur here and can thus testify all the more certainly how poorly things are going on our **hemisphere** <note>original: *hemispherio*</note>.

# Commentaries <note>original: *Commentaria*</note>

...[witnesses the conduct and acts of our world, yet they] were not deterred by our hopefully future **comfort** <note>original: *Confort*</note> and **commerce** <term>Commerciis: trade and social interaction</term>. After they heard what great change and inequality from the first ancient state has occurred in these times with us humans here on our **hemisphere** <note>original: *hemispherio*</note> above, and how almost everything has turned around and fallen into the worst state.

For in the beginning, humans, out of pure simplicity and piety—according to the nature created in them by God—held all things **in common** <term>Gemein: referring to a communal or shared social structure</term> among themselves. They lived together like brothers and sisters and children of one father, from whom they also learned and were instructed in such loyalty and integrity. These carried the name: "What is mine is thine; what is thine is mine." Of this race, only a very small remnant remains and has survived in the world.

These later began to divide themselves, to engage in **commerce** <note>original: *commercia*</note> and trade, leaving the communal life behind and giving one another goods for goods—leather for metal, grain for salt—just as today **remnants** <note>original: *reliquiæ*</note> of that same race still exist in **India** <note>likely referring generally to the East Indies or distant exotic lands</note>, and among the wild **Lapps** <note>the Sámi people of northern Scandinavia</note> in **Sweden**, and elsewhere in the world in various places. They trade loyally and without danger, and know little of the world's **malice** <note>original: *Boßheit*</note>, cheating, and unfaithfulness; although they have already caught a taste and trial of it.

# ...About the Little Peasant <note>original: *vber den kleinen Bawren*</note>

...thus, as time went on, they increasingly allowed themselves to be pleased by **private property** <term>eygenthumb: individual ownership of land or goods, as opposed to communal sharing</term>, to use it strictly, and for each to conduct trade for himself. And regardless of the fact that they initially placed pile against pile <note>referring to the practice of bartering equivalent piles of different goods</note> in their **exchange** <term>abwechslung: the act of swapping or bartering</term>, they nevertheless overcame one another in advantage, and finally, some piles became quite large, others very small, and thus a very great inequality arose from it.

These people followed this rhyme: What is mine, is mine? What is yours, is yours.

Since the **exchange of things** <note>original Latin: *commutatio rerum*</note> and the exchange of **goods** <note>original: *Waaren*</note> did not please some—as they were not satisfied with daily, necessary, and sufficient maintenance for their bodies, their children, and their kin—but instead stretched their thoughts, senses, and spirits further out toward how they might enrich themselves, lift their heads above their other brothers, and come to a position of power: These people invented **money** <term>Gelt: currency or coin used as a medium of exchange</term> (which had to be made from a precious commodity and material that is not obtainable everywhere—that is, from **gold** and **silver**—so that not everyone could attain it). This was to be like a hook <note>original: *angel*, metaphorically a fishing hook or a central pivot</note> in which their and all other trades would go and hover to and fro; by which means and invention they could also trade at a distance and throughout the world, make their piles even larger, and also get behind many other things that are unknown to the **common man** <note>original: *gemeiner Man*; the ordinary citizen or laborer</note> and impossible for him to attain without such means, and thus they could fulfill the desire and purpose of their hearts.

# On the Little Peasant
<note>This likely refers to "Der Kleine Bauer" (The Little Peasant), a famous alchemical treatise by Johann Grasshoff that advocates for a simple, natural approach to the Great Work.</note>

<meta>catchword: will be [wirds]</meta>

...possess or even know. We, however, do this with great understanding and primarily desire the **Center** <note>original: *Centri*</note>. We have no rest, nor any benefit from our labor, until we reach this and possess it. To follow and work according to the **plumb-line** <note>original: *Pleyrecht*; a tool used by masons to ensure a perfect vertical line, here used as a symbol for natural law.</note> is nothing other than to follow **Nature** and let her take her course. For when one follows the plumb-line in building and working, and lets Nature take her course, she shows us the way so that we certainly arrive at the **Center** and do not miss it by a hair's breadth; for Nature cannot fail, provided you do not hinder her or push her to one side. Nature and the **plumb-bob** <note>original: *perpendiculum*</note> always desire the **center of the world** <note>original: *Centri mundi*</note> of their own accord; you need not force or drive them, for it cannot go or fall in any other way.

Therefore, there is nothing easier on Earth than to carry out this **Philosophical Work** <note>The alchemical process of creating the Philosopher's Stone.</note>; one does not even need to lift a finger, but rather let Nature work alone, and watch the process with delight. And when it is finished, one says to Nature with a single word: "Stand still; step aside, and let me possess and enjoy that which you have prepared and upon which you have labored so long," for that is the will of God.

Therefore, all **Artists** <note>In this context, *Artisten* refers to alchemists or practitioners of the Hermetic Art.</note> must, out of necessity, follow the **plumb-line** (which is a cord from which a block of lead or a stone is hung at the bottom; the Philosophers call it **white lead** <term>plumbum album: a term often signifying lead that has been purified or weathered into a white oxide</term>, though it is actually just the common black lead that other craftsmen, builders, and mortar-mixers also use; but when it stands long in the weather...

<summary>This page argues that alchemy is an effortless, natural process modeled on the mechanics of a plumb-line seeking the earth's center. The author claims that the alchemist merely observes Nature's work until it reaches completion by divine will.</summary>

it will be) and it is impossible that the **plumb-bob** <note>original: *Perpendiculum*</note>, once it is struck and not held back, but allowed to swing freely, should miss the **center of the world** <note>original: *Centri mundi*</note>. For Nature, of her own accord, always approaches this center and desires her goal and destined end, for which every **created thing** <note>original: *Creatum*</note> is ordained by its **Creator** <note>original: *Schöpffer*</note>. She does not rest, but (unless hindered) steps ever forward. Thus, in the **Philosophical Work** <note>The alchemical process of creating the Philosopher's Stone.</note>, the beginnings—which stand in a quite wide **space** <note>original: *spatio*</note> from one another—along with the **lines** <note>original: *lineæ*</note> and the **differing elements** <note>original: *discrepierende Elementa*</note>, draw ever closer together during the course of **sublimation** <note>A process of heating a substance until it vapors and then solidifies again, used here to describe the refinement of the work.</note>, the longer it lasts, until they finally converge upon a single point. This point is the **center of the earth** <note>original: *Centrum terræ*</note>, which is so greatly desired, and where so many wonders are said to lie. At that point, make them stand still, once you have all the **lines** <note>original: *lineas*</note> together in this one spot—those lines which strike inward from every direction from the **circumference** <note>original: *circumferenʒ*</note>. For if one allowed them to run further, and you wanted to go deeper down—since these are not **parallel lines** <note>original: *parallelæ*</note> but **plumb lines** <note>original: *lineę perpendiculares*; lines moving directly toward the center.</note> which form **acute angles** <note>original: *angulos acutos*</note> and intersect one another—one would pass with them through the cross. Therefore, if you were to continue outward beyond the middle point with the aforementioned lines, just as quickly as they previously rushed together toward the single middle point, just as quickly—as soon as they crossed the **center of the circle** <note>original: *Centrum circuli*</note> or of the earth—they would immediately open up again, **disperse**, and the longer they go, the further apart they would come once more. They would run **into infinity** <note>original: *in infinitum*</note> in an increasing **divergence** <note>original: *discrepanʒ*</note>; as is the case in all things arising from the **circumference**...

...would seem impossible to an ignorant person. They achieve this, however, through the compass and through an art which is called—taking its name, I believe, from the Greek—*Schinen* <term>Schinen: from the Greek *schoinion*, referring to a measuring line or cord; the early art of mine surveying or "dialing."</term>. 

This is particularly necessary when one wishes to know exactly where they are positioned within the mountains <term>Gebürg: the geological mass or mountain range being mined</term> and how far away the neighboring mine still lies; or whether a breakthrough between two mines is to be hoped for, so that fresh air <note>original: *wetter*; in mining, this refers to ventilation and the management of "damps" or gases.</note> might be brought into the mountain, or otherwise so that the water might be drained out through a neighboring gallery <term>Stollen: a horizontal tunnel driven into a hillside for access or drainage</term>, or for other various reasons. 

The art consists of this: first, inside the mountain (two or three persons are required for this task), they traverse all galleries and shafts <term>Schacht: a vertical or steeply inclined passage connecting different levels of a mine</term>. By means of the magnet or compass, they take certain knowledge and records from one place to another using a taut cord or common sighting. They record the hour <note>Historical mining compasses used a 24-hour scale rather than degrees to indicate direction.</note> on the compass toward which the currently entered gallery—or that specific section of the gallery—stretches along its length. 

As soon as a sighting has occurred, they note it precisely <note>original: *in puncto*</note> in the small writing tablet <term>Schreibtafel: a portable ledger used by surveyors to record measurements in the field</term> they have at hand. One then immediately proceeds through that same gallery (which may be crooked in some places or run straight for a considerable length of cord in others). As far as one can maintain a line of sight by candlelight—or extend the cord, depending on the curvature of the gallery—one likewise takes the direction of that specific section on the compass as a note <note>original: *ad notam*</note> and records it in the writing tablet. This process is carried out from place to place through all the galleries, down to the lowest and final corner where the hewer <term>Hewer: the skilled miner who works at the face, physically cutting the ore from the rock</term> or laborer has his current work site.

# Regarding the Small Mine-Works

When, in such a manner, the entire mine—and all its location and condition, including its length, curvature, and depth—has been most diligently investigated through the various hours <note>Mining compasses of this era were divided into 24 hours rather than 360 degrees to denote direction.</note> of the compass, and simultaneously recorded inside the mountain: then one ascends and transfers all the observations <note>original: *observationes*</note> of the compass recorded below in the mountain, and the lines taken as notes <note>original: *ad notas*</note> from the writing tablet, out into the daylight <note>original: *am Tag*; a mining term for the surface world above the pit.</note> onto the meadows or some other open, level space. There, with staked markers, one recreates above what was found below, from one section and sighting to the next. 

No matter how strangely the galleries <term>Stollen: horizontal mine passages driven for access or drainage</term>, bends <term>Krück: turns or zig-zags in the tunnel where it follows a mineral vein</term>, and shafts <term>Schächte: vertical passages</term> might wind themselves in the deepest parts of the mountain, if the surveyor <term>Schiner: a specialist in the art of subterranean measurement</term> is experienced in the art, diligent, and careful, he can accurately and unfailingly draft the layout, course, and bearings <note>original: *stunden*; literally "hours," referring to compass directions.</note> of the entire mine, as well as those of the neighboring mines, on a flat surface. In this way, anyone may have the entire mine—with all its characteristics—before their eyes, along with the neighboring mine, which must be handled and mapped out <note>original: *zu Platz schlagen*; to mark or stake out a site on the surface to determine boundaries.</note> in the same way from beginning to end, so that one may have and know the distance <note>original: *distants*</note> between both neighboring mines. The mine manager <term>Schichtmeister: the technical and administrative head of a mining operation</term>, in the name of the common shareholders <term>Gewercken: individuals who owned shares in a mine and were responsible for its costs and entitled to its profits</term>, comes before the mining judge <term>Bergrichter: a legal official who oversaw mining titles and adjudicated disputes</term> to settle and reach agreements with one another. Indeed, they often choose to merge two disputed mines into a single company so that they might share the expenses, build more robustly, and await equal fortune or loss in the name of God.

In this way, these noble miners, through their workings and immovable properties, do no harm to any other people who conduct their business above on the surface <note>original: *superficie*</note>. And it is not said here: "What this man has in excess, the other must lack." In the world above, the territory is narrow and the people and "brothers" are many; the wealthy seize all the property for themselves, so that the common citizen can hardly sustain himself anymore or acquire and purchase his own goods, etc. 

Not so here: Here there is field <meta>The catchword "Felds" (field) from the previous page provides continuity for this sentence.</meta> enough. For here, a vast, immeasurable, and unworked field lies open beneath the mountain. Every person is free to prospect <note>original: *schürpffen*; to search for ore by digging trial pits</note> where they wish, to set hammer and chisel <term>Schlegel vnd Eysen: the two primary hand tools of the miner, which became the universal symbol of the trade</term> to the rock, and to seek a vein which they believe to be richest for several miles around, driving their tunnel <term>Stollen: a horizontal passage driven into a hillside for drainage or access</term> toward it. 

He may start a new mine <term>Bergwerck: the physical site and legal entity of a mining operation</term>, or—either alone or with a good partner—revive and lease an old pit, or enter into an ongoing operation with another company and its shareholders through a proper purchase, sharing in common profit or loss according to his hope of striking ore <term>Ertz: the raw, metal-bearing mineral</term>. # Concerning the Little Peasant

...[of various] creatures remaining, [God] has inserted that same **Spirit** <note>original: *Spiritum*</note> into this mass, preserved and deeply locked away at the bottom of the mountain’s crevices. He has left it for the **Philosophers** <note>original: *Philosophis*, referring here to practitioners of alchemy</note> to raise up, prepare, and use, and to perform similar **miracles** <note>original: *miracula*</note> with it—and He still equips and implants it daily.

Whenever this prepared **Stone** <note>original: *Lapidem*</note> of the Philosophers is held against another imperfect or inferior metal—or when it touches such a metal while it is in a liquid state <term>Fluß: the molten state of metal during smelting</term>—it immediately, within a quarter of an hour, or rather, in the blink of an eye, turns that same metal into pure, high-grade fine silver or fine gold.

And since such pious and God-loving men commonly keep only a tenth part of the resulting gold and silver for themselves and their own persons—to provide for their physical needs or, if they please, for other praiseworthy things—while devoting the remaining nine parts to relieving the needs of the poor, would you still grumble about it? Would you still despise this hearty and glorious **Art** <note>original: *Kunst*, the "Great Art" of alchemy</note>, or deny it its praise, dignity, and justice? Should you not much rather help to exalt it above all other outward **Gifts of God** <note>original: *Gaaben Gottes*</note> and allow it to pass as such?

And if you say: "Where are these people? I see none! If one of them would perform a trial just once, using several **hundredweight** <note>original: *Centner*, a traditional unit of weight</note> of material, then I too would begin to believe."

And he thinks it would be much better if one made a whole **peppercorn sack** <note>original: *Pfeffersack* - a metaphor for a very large quantity, often used to describe the bulky merchandise of wealthy traders.</note> full right at the start, rather than dealing with tiny **drachms** <term>quintlen: A small unit of weight, roughly 3.6 grams.</term> and **half-ounces** <term>lohten: A 'Lot' was a traditional German unit of weight, approximately 15–17 grams.</term>; then one would have a supply for a while, and it would take the same labor, and almost the same time and expense. For to make a great deal of the "good thing" in the first attempt, or to weigh it out for the **composition** <note>original: *Composition* - the precise combining of alchemical ingredients.</note> and then to mix it, is an almost impossible or at least a very difficult thing. There is a reason for this, which is unnecessary to speak of further here. You surely know well enough otherwise that sometimes a small trial succeeds, but one can no longer find success in a large quantity of that same material.

You may nonetheless set up several or a few glasses at certain times at the start—not for the sake of a great quantity of the **tincture**, but for other reasons: so that, if you are sleeping, you might be woken up by a **bang** <note>Alchemical vessels were prone to exploding under pressure; the author humorously suggests this serves as an alarm clock.</note>, or perhaps one might boil over and sit in the ashes, or else so that you may have your **observations** <note>original: *Observationes*</note>, **reasons** <note>original: *rationes*</note>, pleasure, and wonder.

But that only a very small portion is obtained at the beginning does not concern the Master; for, however small a start he has, it will come to fruition later, if he is not entirely weary...

...to be brief, as we have conversed with each other a little about this **Little Peasant** and exchanged words in writing, until we may one day come to him ourselves and speak to that **highly enlightened man** <note>This likely refers to the author of the "Little Peasant" treatise or the symbolic figure representing the alchemical process itself.</note> in person; and should he still be living, enjoy his company, for it was only twenty years ago that he held discourse with his man.

Since my first draft <note>original: *gestö / Schrifft* — likely referring to a rough or "pounded out" draft.</note> seemed to sound much too clear—at which I myself was startled while reading—I corrected the argument myself. I will present in few words what alchemy is and how the Stone <term>Lapis</term> <note>original: *Lapis* — The Philosophers' Stone.</note> is made. And this, I hope, without lies. So hear now: The first material of the philosophers is not common mercury <term>Mercurius vulgi</term> <note>original: *Mercurius vulgi* — literally "mercury of the common folk," referring to ordinary quicksilver as opposed to the refined "mercury of the philosophers."</note>; instead, it is an essence <term>Essentz</term> which is extracted from common mercury with much time and great care. And when the aforementioned essence of common mercury is thus prepared and ready, and has become a beautiful sublimate <term>sublimat</term> <note>A substance purified through heating into a vapor and cooling back into a solid.</note> that looks like a beautiful, shining mirror from which pearls <term>uniones</term> <note>original: *uniones* — a term for large, high-quality pearls, here describing the lustrous appearance of the chemical substance.</note> shine forth:

Then one mixes the sulfur or tincture of the Sun <term>Tinctur Solis</term> <note>original: *Tinctur Solis* — alchemical code for the essence of gold.</note> into it, at the proper weight, and thus makes from these two parts a compound <term>Compositum</term>: (which composition must nevertheless be undertaken not according to arithmetic proportion, but according to geometric proportion <note>original: *secundum propositionem Arithmeticam, sonder Geometricam* — This implies the ratio is based on the "virtue" or quality of the materials rather than simple volume or weight.</note>, as we have also heard above in its proper place) and it is soon calcined <term>calcioniert</term> <note>The process of reducing a substance to a powder through intense heat.</note> with the strongest fire; thus it becomes a powder. And when the calcination is over, the material is fixed <term>fix</term>, entirely fire-resistant and incombustible, and it no longer causes a heavy heart <note>original: *vmb kein bösen Herzen* — an idiom suggesting the material is now stable and will no longer cause the alchemist anxiety through failure or volatility.</note> for anyone, neither for itself nor for its master. Such virtue and property must the Stone, which is to hold the volatile mercury and perform and accomplish other wonders, always possess. And when it has now been brought to such fixedness <term>fixitet</term>, it is indeed still white; but one must burn it further until it becomes red. And—in order that it might become easily melted and more refined (certainly, for those who wish)—pour over it several times with sharp waters <term>scharppfen Wasseren</term> <note>Refers to strong acids or chemical solvents used for purification.</note>: then it begins to prove its power...

# Commentaria

[Knowledge] creates the [understanding of] incoming pieces <note>referring to ingredients</note> that one puts into the pot, the **knowledge and proportion of ingredients** <note>original: *noticia & proportio Ingredientium*</note>, from which one prepares and composes every dish <term>Geköcht</term> <note>A general term for a dish, decoction, or something being cooked.</note> before coming to the fire with it: Or also, when it has already stood by the fire for a time, what one intends to throw in during the cooking. Which knowledge one must either take from cookbooks or learn from experienced cooks: Therefore one also lets the young cooks wander, sending them here and there to the courts of Princes, for the types of gourmets <term>Schleckmäuler</term> <note>literally "lick-mouths," referring to those with refined or demanding palates</note> are many.

Now when one has learned the art and has sufficient knowledge, then secondly a diligence is also required, so that a proper cook subsequently watches his fire and his dish, so that nothing is burned, nothing over-salted, also dressed in the proper manner, nothing over-spiced, nothing over-vinegared or even over-wined: and when necessity requires it, fresh water is poured into the reduction, and the broth is maintained in the proper **consistency** <note>original: *Consistenz*</note>: So that instead of a tasty meal, which should lovably affect the tongue and palate of the one enjoying it, strengthen the body and maintain health, there does not arise from the ruined and poorly tended dish a **nausea** <note>original: *nausea* — a feeling of sickness or loathing.</note> and distaste. Where this diligence is not present, the art of cooking and the knowledge help nothing: Therefore there are also so many slovenly cooks <term>Sudelköch</term> <note>A derogatory term for messy, unskilled, or "greasy spoon" cooks.</note>.

Also it is not the least trick, nor the worst art in cooking, that, if the cook out of igno[rance]— <note>The text cuts off mid-word, likely "unwissenheit" (ignorance).</note>

### Commentaries

when they are about to serve it and the greens <note>original: "Kraut", which can refer to herbs, cabbage, or leafy vegetables.</note> are scorched and sticking to the pot <term>Hafen</term> <note>A traditional deep ceramic or metal cooking vessel.</note>, they immediately run for water, place the pot in cold water, and then smear tallow <term>Unschlitt</term> <note>Animal fat, usually from sheep or oxen, used for cooking or as a sealant.</note> on the sides. They also grab a water-pan, dip it into cold water, and hold it upside down for a while over the pot; this is meant to take away and draw out the scorched smell <term>Brand</term>. Others quickly move it into a fresh pot and pour a little more water in, etc. **You do likewise** <note>original: "Tu fac similiter."</note>. For most errors <note>original: "errores"</note> that occur in the progress of the work <note>original: "progressu operis"</note> among the careless must be corrected and set right with water.

I have before this time read these words in an old book: **In the regulation of fire, almost all alchemical cooks have erred** <note>original: "In regimine ignis omnes ferè erraverunt coci alchemistici."</note>. These words, although they have their own specific <note>original: "in specie"</note> and secret meaning, generally point toward that which almost all philosophers <note>original: "Philosophi", here referring to alchemists.</note> have preached and warned their successors and the seekers of this art: that they should watch and act with caution, not to apply heat too suddenly, so as not to burn the decoction <term>Geköchts</term> <note>The substance currently being boiled or processed in the vessel.</note>.

> Zeno in the *Assembly* <note>original: "Zinon in turba", referring to the *Turba Philosophorum*, one of the oldest Latin alchemical texts.</note>: If anyone introduced to this art knew its nature, he would certainly endure the long duration of the cooking until, by the will of God, he extracted his purpose.

> The Lily <note>original: "Lilium", likely referring to the *Lilium Intelligentiae*, an alchemical treatise.</note>: Know that without heat nothing is ever generated, and that intense heat causes the composite to perish and flee; but through tempered fire, the body becomes sweet and harmonious.

Morienus <note>A legendary 7th-century alchemist and hermit.</note> says: The craftsman should know the kindling of his fire; that is one thing <note>original: "Sciat Artifex sui ignis accensionem, ist eins."</note>. And let it endure with an equal burning through its days; that is the third <note>original: "Et per suos dies æqualis ardendo perduret, ists dritt."</note>.

Bonellus in the *Assembly of Philosophers* <note>original: "Turba [Philosophorum]," one of the oldest and most influential Latin alchemical texts.</note> says: "Truly, in it is that which amends it, unless it is driven away by excessive fire and excessive haste" <note>original: "Revera in eo est, quod ipsum emendet, nisi fugetur igne nimio ac nimia festinantia."</note>.

And most philosophers recommend a mild fire, and testify with one voice that haste is of the Devil <note>original: "festinantia sit à Diabolo."</note>.

But regarding what specific inconvenience, damage, and disaster results when one adopts the manner and ways of the disobedient "slop-cooks" <term>Sudelköche</term> <note>A derogatory term for careless or fraudulent alchemists who work without theoretical knowledge.</note> and wishes to be done with it quickly: the wise masters say that through this, the material becomes vitrified <term>vitrificiert</term> <note>Turned into a glass-like slag or cinder that cannot be easily processed further.</note>, which afterwards can either not be brought to solution <term>solution</term> <note>The process of dissolving a solid back into a liquid state.</note> at all, or only with great difficulty.

And it is written regarding the universal way <term>via universali</term> <note>The standard path to creating the Philosopher's Stone.</note>: if the fire is too great, then the moist spirit <term>Spiritus</term> <note>The volatile essence or "soul" of the chemical substance.</note> flies away (or is consumed, and is not applied as is right, but is forced with violence into the body <term>corpus</term> or earth <term>terra</term>. But whatever is driven in by force is not natural, nor is it as good, fixed <note>Refers to "fixity," the ability of a substance to withstand fire without evaporating.</note>, and stable as when it proceeds slowly and with gentleness); or else the vessel might break, and the subtle spirit departs into the air. A temperate fire preserves the radical moisture <term>humiditas radicalis</term> <note>The essential, life-giving moisture believed to hold the "seed" of metals.</note>; an excessive one consumes it <note>original: "Temperatus ignis humiditatem radicalem conservat, nimius consumit."</note>.

It also deprives it of its entry <term>Ingreß</term> <note>The ability of the alchemical medicine to penetrate and transform base metals.</note> during the projection <term>Projection</term> <note>The final stage of alchemy where the Philosopher's Stone is cast upon a molten metal to transmute it.</note>, for with such unbridled fire the Stone <term>Lapis</term> by no means becomes fusible <term>fusibilis</term> <note>Able to be melted or dissolved into the metal.</note>, which is what must happen in every way

->### ELUCIDATION OF THE TESTAMENT OF RAY- mond Lull. <note>original: "ELVCIDATIO TESTAMENTI RAY- mundi Lullij"; Raymond Lull (c. 1232–1315) was a Majorcan philosopher, though many alchemical texts using his name were written by later followers</note> ###<-

Although we have composed many books on various operations of our philosophical art: nonetheless, we prefer this, our last little book, to all the others, which deserves to be titled the ***Elucidation*** <note>original: "Elucidatio"</note> ***of the Testament*** by us: because that which we hide with great lengthiness in our philosophical writings in our ***Testament*** and ***Codicil*** <note>Two of the most famous alchemical works attributed to Lull</note>: we show more clearly and elucidate most briefly in this little book of ours: so that there is no further need to compose other books. Since the composition of our books is nothing other than the subtlety of a keen mind for the purpose of concealing our art—which, though shown abundantly in our books, is here led from the darkness into a pleasant light—something which no philosopher ever dared to do with such boldness. ### Chapter One: Concerning the Matter of Our Stone.

First, therefore, let us proceed to demonstrate the matter of our ***Stone*** <note>The Philosopher’s Stone, the legendary substance believed to facilitate the transmutation of metals and the prolongation of life</note>. For we have introduced foreign things into our mastery through their likenesses, even though there exists but one single thing for our stone, to which we add no outside matter, nor do we take anything away. We have also described three Stones—namely the ***Mineral***, ***Animal***, and ***Vegetable***—when in truth there is but one stone of our art. We wish, O sons, for this composite to signify three things: namely, ***body***, ***soul***, and ***spirit***. It is called "mineral" because it comes from a mine; "animal" because it possesses a soul; and "vegetable" because it grows and multiplies. In this lies the entire secret of our mastery, which is ***Sun*** <note>symbolizing Gold</note>, ***Moon*** <note>symbolizing Silver</note>, and the ***water of life***. And the ***water of life*** is the soul and the life of bodies, through which our stone is quickened <note>original: "vivificatur"; brought to life</note> and sustained <note>original: "supplantatur"; in alchemical Latin, this often refers to being supported or established from a foundation</note>; therefore we call it ***heaven***, and the ***quintessence*** <note>term: "quinta essentia"; the "fifth element" or purest essence beyond earth, air, fire, and water</note>, and ***incombustible oil***, and by infinite other names: because it is almost as incorruptible as the heavens in the continual circulation of its motion. Thus, in a clear demonstration free from all wandering words, you have the matter of our stone.

## Chapter Four: Concerning Fire.

Although we have treated triple fire—namely **natural**, **connatural**, and **unnatural** <term>unnatural fire</term> <note>term: "ignis contra naturam"; literally "fire against nature." ### *Chapter Five: Concerning Decoction.* <term>decoction</term> <note>decoctio; the process of heating or "cooking" a substance to bring it to maturity or to extract its essence.</note>

There are also many ways of preparing our stone <term>stone</term> <note>lapis; the Philosopher's Stone, the legendary substance capable of transmuting metals and granting long life.</note> described in our *Testament* and our other volumes: namely, solution, coagulation, sublimation, distillation, calcination <term>calcination</term> <note>calcinatio; the process of heating a solid to high temperatures to remove volatile substances or reduce it to a fine powder.</note>, separation, fusion, inceration <note>the process of softening a substance until it has a wax-like consistency</note>, imbibition <note>the slow absorption of a liquid by a solid matter</note>, fixation, and so on. The true significance of all these processes is **decoction**. For in our decoction alone are all these various methods perfected. 

The method of our decoction is this: you place the matter of the composite, according to its measure, into its vessel, furnace, and fire, boiling it continuously until it reaches the completion of maturity. This will be achieved in ten months without any manual labor <note>The author suggests that once the "fire" is set, the alchemist does not need to physically manipulate the substance; the heat performs the work naturally over time.</note>, from the beginning until the end of the entire Great Work <term>Great Work</term> <note>magisterium; the successful completion of the alchemical process.</note>. However, we intend for these assigned methods to signify the sublimity of our art, and to ensure that the understanding of the foolish remains surrounded by shadows...

### *Chapter Six: Concerning the Tincture and Multiplication of our Stone.*

Finally, we shall speak of the tincture and multiplication, which is the end and completion of the whole mastery <term>mastery</term> <note>magisterij; the entire alchemical process or "Great Work" (Magnum Opus).</note>. For we have shown many forms of the modes of projection <term>projection</term> <note>proiectio; the final step of the alchemical process where the finished Stone is "cast" upon base metals to transform them into gold or silver.</note> for our tincture <term>tincture</term> <note>tinctura; the concentrated power of the Stone to "color" or transform the nature of a substance.</note> in our volumes, though our tincture is not different from multiplication, and neither of these can occur without the other. This is because our stone does not tinge unless it is first tinged, and when it is tinged, its quantity is multiplied. And with our stone multiplied—whether white or red <note>The "white" stone was said to produce silver, while the "red" stone produced gold.</note>—the work is tinged. O son, cast away the shadows of the intellect to understand the secret of secrets <note>arcanorum arcanum</note>, hidden in our books with skillful diligence, which is here brought up from the depths into the heights.

Hear and understand that our multiplication <term>multiplication</term> <note>multiplicatio; the method of increasing the potency and quantity of the Philosopher's Stone through repeated refining.</note> is nothing other than the reiteration <term>reiteration</term> <note>reiteratio; the repetition of the previous stages of the work to "ripen" the Stone further.</note> of our primordial composite work. For in the first reiteration, one part of our stone tinges three parts of the "imperfect body" <note>imperfecti corporis; refers to base metals like lead or mercury that are seen as "sick" or unfinished versions of gold.</note>, and it grows and multiplies in quantity by that many parts. In the second reiteration, one part tinges seven parts. In the third, one part tinges fifteen. In the fourth, thirty-one. In the fifth, 63. In the sixth, 127.

...for it is a gift of God the Most High / of that you can be certain. And now listen: we shall seat ourselves upon this greenery. For I am old / and by nature cold: I also have an injury in my legs / therefore I cannot stand for long: moreover / I also like to rest in the green.
